title: Pennsylvania’s Public-Health Officials May Be Wrong About a Measles Death
excerpt: Measles outbreaks around the country are already a disaster, but more bad news arrived on Tuesday
body: Measles outbreaks around the country are already a disaster, but more bad news arrived on Tuesday

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro announced that two measles-associated deaths had occurred in Lancaster County. “These mark the first deaths related to measles within the Commonwealth in 35 years,” an accompanying statement declared
Both individuals were said to have been unvaccinated, but the state Health Department declined to release any other information about the cases, citing privacy concerns
By yesterday morning, though, this story was in doubt
Lancaster County Commissioner Josh Parsons posted on X that he had spoken with the county’s coroner, who said that he had not identified any deaths due to measles
One individual, Parsons wrote, “died WITH measles, but not from measles.” That evening, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F

Kennedy Jr. offered a more conspiratorial angle: Perhaps the entire episode had been “fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers.” Pennsylvania’s Health Department quickly doubled down : “As a pediatrician with more than 30 years of caring for children,” the state’s health secretary wrote, “I have thoroughly reviewed the case investigation information and sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County.” But the facts that have emerged over the past 48 hours suggest that health officials may indeed have committed a catastrophic communication blunder—by either overstating the evidence or politicizing the deaths of citizens without conveying complete information about what had happened

Here’s what we know so far: In the one case for which additional information has been released, an infant whose lab tests showed evidence of a measles infection died shortly after birth because of a lacerated spleen
According to an interview with the county coroner conducted by The Philadelphia Inquirer , a forensic pathologist decided that this fatal injury was not related to the infection
That pathologist’s judgment might be wrong
Viruses (including measles) can cause the spleen to grow abnormally large, making it prone to rupture
A 2024 Polish study , for instance, documented an enlarged spleen in four out of 26 infants who had been hospitalized for measles
But there are certainly other potential explanations
Only a doctor familiar with all of the details of this particular patient’s situation would be equipped to reach a reasonable conclusion
Yet when Shapiro announced the two fatalities, he implied that the link was unambiguous. “Death from measles is completely preventable,” he said
The baby in Lancaster could not have been vaccinated; newborns are not typically given their first dose of the MMR vaccine until they are 1 year old

According to the coroner, the infected newborn acquired the disease in utero from their mother. (Her vaccination status has not been publicly confirmed.) If some genuine uncertainty remains as to whether a measles infection led directly to the baby’s death, state officials’ announcement was premature
Think of the consequences: A grieving parent would hear her governor announce that the tragedy was in some way her fault
And anti-vaccine activists would have the opportunity to pounce on the mistake to continue downplaying the lethality of infections
As a pathologist, I am used to fielding questions about how and why people die
Such calls were particularly frequent during the early days of the coronavirus pandemic, when many people doubted COVID-19’s official death toll

Some alleged that anyone who merely happened to die while infected—in a car crash, let’s say, or from cancer—was being counted in official numbers. (In fact, government statistics were underestimating the number of Americans who were dying from COVID.) Admittedly, determining why someone died is in many cases difficult for experts such as myself
The body is a frustratingly complex machine
A mild illness can lead to a cascade of severe bodily dysfunction; disparate diseases may all crop up simultaneously
Seemingly ill people can live for years, while apparently healthy individuals rapidly deteriorate

And measles, in particular, may pose a special challenge for cause-of-death discernment, because the virus tends to interfere with the body’s normal immune responses , making death from any pathogen more likely. [ Read: Yes, some children may have died from COVID shots ] Doctors have developed a specialized language to convey these nuances
Many people end up having two listed causes of death: an immediate cause and an underlying cause

The immediate cause is the disease process that was most closely related to a fatal malfunction of a patient’s heart, lungs, or brain; the underlying cause is the event that initiated a patient’s decline

The Pennsylvania Health Department has said that it uses the term measles-associated death when measles infection is present but may not be the “immediate cause of death.” To see how this works, consider the deaths of two children from measles in Texas last year
Anti-vaccine activists seized on the fact that these kids had both died after contracting non-measles infections to cast doubt on the conclusion that measles was the cause
In fact, this is the typical way that measles kills: The virus weakens a patient’s body, allowing harmful bacteria or viruses to take hold more easily
Bacterial pneumonia or sepsis may have been the children’s immediate cause of death—but measles was the underlying cause
The situation does not seem to be as clear-cut in Pennsylvania
A fatal splenic injury caused by a congenital measles infection may be plausible, but it would not be a typical cause of death from the disease
And regardless of whether measles unequivocally led to either of the two deaths in Pennsylvania, officials have already emboldened vaccine skeptics and lent credibility to their doubts

The state Health Department seems to have withheld relevant information from its constituents—that is, that local investigators were not themselves attributing the infant’s death to measles—and then it politicized its announcement of the deaths by having Shapiro, who is currently running for reelection, play a prominent role in the press conference. (In response to questions, Stephanie Nojiri, the deputy press secretary for the health department, directed me to the health secretary’s prior statement

She declined to provide any further details about the cases, again citing patient confidentiality.) [ Read: Do childhood vaccines cause tornadoes? ] Public-health experts should have known that the anti-vaccine movement would use any modicum of ambiguity in the evidence to press its case
Kennedy himself has been doing this for years

In 2021, he called the idea that “measles is a deadly disease” propaganda, and visited an Amish fair in Lancaster County to congratulate locals on their wariness toward vaccines (“The Amish are doing it right,” he said ), make light of measles’ risks, and tout chicken soup and vitamin A as its cure
Kennedy has repeatedly denied having any responsibility for measles outbreaks

title: Everything Is Called America Now
excerpt: “If you think about it, we have a gulf, and we have a lake
body: “If you think about it, we have a gulf, and we have a lake
Now all we need is an ocean.” — President Trump, declaring Lake Ontario “Lake America” via executive order The year is 2027
Gas costs $83 a gallon, and lettuce is at war with us
However, every location on every map is now labeled America

Sometimes for fun we hike from the Trump Airport to the other Trump Airport to the other Trump Airport. (The few remaining air-traffic controllers have taken up heavy smoking from all the stress and confusion.) We do not fly; it is too expensive, and the planes don’t know where they’re going
The good news is that we are still a member of the America America America America (formerly the North Atlantic Treaty Organization)
The renaming clinched it! Maps are functionally useless
What is the deepest point in the American Ocean? Impossible to know
America stretches from one to the other, below the Lakes America (mnemonic acronym: AAAAA)
Every lake is Lake America, and every gulf is the Gulf of America

Our battleships (Trump-class, and all named for former Confederates) are very confused all the time and have been at sea for months; the crews on them are sick and undersupplied. (We would call this a national disgrace but disgrace is now “America” too.) Every kind of cheese is American cheese, even the kind with holes
If tariffs hadn’t made maple syrup (from our northern neighbor, America) so expensive, we would make American waffles
All actors are named America, not just Ferrara
Every kind of bulldog is an American bulldog
There are no Canada geese any more (not due to renaming, due to the Incident)
We eat American muffins and Trump salad (which used to be Caesar)
Sometimes for breakfast we eat an American! (Formerly a Danish
We hope.) We go to American baths. (There is no water in them due to the evaporation of Lake America
The other Lake America.) American kids don’t get measles any longer
They get America! All penguins are now named Donald Trump by law, except the small, disgraceful ones
Every band is America, except for Kid Rock, who received a special exception
Texas toast is still allowed, but Georgia peaches are on thin ice, contingent on electoral outcomes

Inflation? Don’t ask! We have no idea! Numbers are now the word America printed in a tiny font! This makes inflation less noticeable, because no words have any meaning or value anymore! If someone had a particle of backbone, we could at least have legible maps! I’m sorry: if someone had a particle of Trump (we are renaming the body parts too)
American students are now the best at geography because there is only one possible answer to every question
But that’s only in the real world, which is no longer relevant
On the map, everything is America (fine)! Sometimes we want to just go jump into Lake America to get away from it all

title: A Turning Point in AI Writing
excerpt: There was a time—a more innocent age—when you could read an op-ed in a major newspaper and confidently say that a human had written it
body: There was a time—a more innocent age—when you could read an op-ed in a major newspaper and confidently say that a human had written it
Hold on to the memory of that for as long as you can

This week, after the billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller published an editorial in The Wall Street Journal criticizing Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, his onetime protégé, readers began to notice some familiar tics of AI writing
According to Pangram, the AI-detection tool, the op-ed was 100 percent AI-generated
AI writing has regularly snuck into mainstream outlets, and especially newspaper op-ed pages , despite policies against it
Up to now, those accused of passing off a computer’s writing as their own have tended to either apologize or deny it

In April, James Taranto, the Journal ’s editorial-features editor, wrote a column comparing Pangram to a “defamation machine” that was fueling unfounded accusations of AI use, including in op-eds he had overseen. “Those of us who practice writing as a professional craft have an ethical duty, and sometimes a contractual obligation, to ensure that our work is original,” he wrote. [ Read: The most famous AI writing tic is also the most mysterious ] The difference this time is that Druckenmiller owned it. “Of course I used AI,” he told NOTUS on Tuesday. “I’m not embarrassed by it,” he added. “I write everything using AI now for the same reason I use a calculator when I do math problems.” And rather than rebuke him, The Wall Street Journal ’s editorial-page editor, Paul Gigot, defended the practice. “AI is a fact of modern life,” he said in a statement
Last night, Gigot followed up with a full column on the subject, mocking the “media pharisees” who wag their fingers at automated writing

He clarified that the Journal ’s opinion staffers must still draft their own columns and editorials but said that he doesn’t intend to police AI use by outside contributors. “Many contributors, especially prominent politicians or CEOs, employ speechwriters or hire a Beltway writing shop,” he wrote. “How different is that from using AI to streamline an essay?” It’s one thing for Druckenmiller to not be embarrassed; plenty of business and tech tycoons are bullish about AI’s utility for writing and just about everything else. “If Stan Druckenmiller isn’t embarrassed,” the venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya posted on X , “you shouldn’t be either.” Valorizing the process of unassisted human writing is “like after matches was invented, still celebrating the arduous time to rub two sticks together,” Palihapitiya added
However, one of America’s most prestigious newspapers welcoming the technology into its pages is unprecedented
Is AI writing entering its post-shame era? Gigot is not wrong that Druckenmiller’s frankness seems almost refreshing in a moment when so much of the writing world is stuck in denial
And his assertion that an AI-composed essay could reflect a human’s authentic ideas is reasonable
I won’t pretend to know enough about bond markets to assess Druckenmiller’s op-ed on its merits
But it seems to have advanced a substantive and non-obvious argument that broadly reflects his views, regardless of who—or what—strung its words together
Op-eds by public figures are rarely authorial master classes anyway
But the notion that Druckenmiller and Gigot deserve points for honesty overlooks their lack of transparency
Before this week, the one thing everyone in the AI-writing debate still seemed to agree on was the importance of disclosure
The Journal ’s opinion section appears to have blown past that
Druckenmiller’s op-ed contains no indication that he used AI

In his column, Gigot scoffed at the idea that his readers deserve to know when a piece is chatbot-assisted. “Disclose what?” he asked rhetorically. “​​Interrogate an author on how precisely he used ChatGPT? I know some publications claim to do this, but I suspect it’s more pro forma than systematic.” (Gigot did not respond to my requests for comment, nor did a spokesperson for Dow Jones, the Journal ’s parent company

Taranto told me via email that he stands by his April op-ed and believes that Gigot’s statements are consistent with what he wrote.) If the Journal ’s higher-ups really believe that their readers don’t care whether an op-ed was written by AI, what would be the harm in letting them know when it is? In fact, studies have found that readers sometimes prefer ChatGPT’s prose or short stories to the human variety—but sour on them when informed about the AI’s involvement
Gigot might conclude from this that people actually like AI writing and just don’t realize it yet
Another interpretation is that people would rather spend their limited time on prose that emanated from another human mind

Perhaps outsourcing an op-ed to a chatbot isn’t materially different from outsourcing it to a ghostwriter. (Although if that’s the case, maybe we should question the practice of ghostwriting before using it to justify AI.) In any circumstance, the Journal ’s leap from nuh-uh to so what? feels premature
Yes, many transformative technologies have overcome opposition on their way to broad acceptance, but that doesn’t mean the resistance is a waste of time
It’s part of how society hashes out norms, sets limits, and buys time to adapt
Publishing AI writing under a human byline without telling anyone seems more likely to erode people’s trust in the technology than build it

There’s another reason to keep up the norm of disclosure: When people let a chatbot do their writing—even if they’re guiding and carefully reviewing its work—they might not realize that it’s doing some of their thinking too

Jenna Russell, a doctoral candidate in computer science at the University of Maryland who has studied AI writing in newspapers , told me that her colleagues’ latest line of inquiry involves “argument collapse.” In a paper that has yet to be peer-reviewed, Maryland researchers found that AI-written essays are far less likely to advance novel points than those written entirely by humans. “These LLMs can start to affect our ideologies without our consciously knowing that it’s happening,” Russell said
Maybe Druckenmiller owning his AI use and receiving the Journal’ s blessing heralds a new era of guilt-free mechanized writing
Or maybe it’s just another example of the rich and powerful getting away with something that others can’t

Gigot’s defense of Druckenmiller suggested that his reputation and stature obviated concerns about his use of AI. “His contribution to the public debate was still valuable, and he’s welcome in our pages any time,” Gigot wrote

In contrast, when a previously obscure writer, Mia Ballard, was accused of using AI in her horror novel Shy Girl , her publisher launched an investigation, canceled the book, and left her reputation in shreds
How this plays out for the Journal and the rest of the industry will probably depend, aptly enough, on market forces
If people really are willing to pay for opinions articulated by chatbots, other publications are likely to follow suit
They’ll have no shortage of submissions from writers eager to turn a few prompts into a published op-ed.

title: Watching Tim Curry Have Fun Was the Most Fun Thing
excerpt: As a performer, Tim Curry knew how to walk a fine line
body: As a performer, Tim Curry knew how to walk a fine line
Even his most sinister characters had an ironic sort of appeal, because watching Curry have fun is, in itself, fun

The actor, who died yesterday at age 80, acted with palpable glee: He could produce a real-life version of the Grinch’s ever-widening grin and could commit to sheer silliness in a way that freed him to twirl around in a cape while singing a gibberish song about Halloween
Perhaps nowhere was this more evident than in the 1985 film Clue

When the raucous comedy adaptation of the classic whodunit board game debuted in theaters, Paramount Pictures had a unique plan: Instead of one ending, the movie would have three, and audiences never knew which resolution—which killer, in which room, with which weapon—they were going to see

How could the studio sell viewers on a story as convoluted as Clue , whose script was designed to keep people guessing until the very last second? By recruiting an ensemble of comedy greats led by Curry, of course

The actor could easily inhabit a character who was neither wholly a hero nor totally a villain, but rather a merrily odd mix of both. [ Read: The absolute pleasure of Tim Curry ] As Wadsworth, the reticent butler observing the deadly dinner party central to Clue , the actor projects calm hauteur
This appearance, however, shows cracks the moment the partygoers start to trickle in
While the guests—each referred to by a colorful pseudonym—chafe against one another and a dastardly murder plot unfolds, you get the sense that Wadsworth almost wishes they’d all drop dead
As the night ticks closer to its big reveal, his eagerness to expose the true villain inches toward giddy

In a film full to the gills with such talented comedic performers as Madeline Kahn, Christopher Lloyd, and Michael McKean, Curry stands out not just because he’s in every scene, but also because he lends Wadsworth his signature edge and too-toothy grin, landing between saucy and ominous
This commitment to silliness was, perhaps paradoxically, why he was able to imbue even his villains with a particular allure
As The Rocky Horror Picture Show ’s mad-scientist master of ceremonies, Dr

Frank-N-Furter, and as the child-eating clown Pennywise in Stephen King’s It , Curry’s best-known characters revel in their strangeness to such a degree that we love watching them on-screen because of—not despite—how frightening they are
His joy in playing these parts always comes across, inviting his audience to share in the merriment
Wadsworth’s true nature is often obscure in Clue , but the murderous impulse is always there—just beneath the stiff collar and eternally rolling eyes
At the story’s climax, Wadsworth delivers, while running from room to room, a nearly 10-minute monologue so intricate that he almost stumbles over his own words
He prods and mocks the surviving partygoers while their anxiety mounts, kicking off cascades of slapstick pratfalls and wry asides
No matter where he took us, or what strange happenings would meet us there when we arrived, following Tim Curry has always been a delight.

title: Why I Am Right About AI
excerpt: Editor’s note: This article was generated by Claude AI in the style of Paul Gigot, the Wall Street Journal opinion-page editor
body: Editor’s note: This article was generated by Claude AI in the style of Paul Gigot, the Wall Street Journal opinion-page editor
Gigot recently published an AI-generated essay using the investor Stanley Druckenmiller’s byline
In the spirit of full disclosure, readers should know that Claude’s work was so banal that human Atlantic editors have added jokes
Human Atlantic copy editors have also fixed a variety of grammatical and style errors
I have been thinking about this for close to 20 minutes, and I have concluded that human writing is finished
Let me begin with an anecdote, because that is how serious arguments begin
Last Tuesday I asked a machine to write me a birthday message for my sister-in-law

If a machine can fool Deborah, I see no reason to believe it cannot fool the rest of you. (My sister-in-law’s name is Linda, but the machine called her Deborah, so now I do, too.) Some will object to my obviously correct argument
They will say that a birthday message to Deborah is not the same as a novel or a newspaper article
To which I say: Isn’t it, though? Both are made of words
That is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the entire argument, and I would encourage critics to sit with it before responding
It doesn’t matter what any of the words are or what order they’re in
There is a difference in the quantity of words between a birthday card and a novel, and quantity is precisely the thing machines are best at

I consider the matter settled but will continue for another 900 words because that is what the prompt demanded of me—and because a word count is itself a kind of literature now, according to the DOGE subcommittee I just invented at the newspaper that I would like to destroy
I will not elaborate on it, but do consider it
The historical record is entirely on my side, and I say this without having consulted it
There was a time when men delivered ice to houses
There was a time when people made their own candles
The candle situation and the ice situation are, structurally, identical to literature, and anyone who says otherwise is being sentimental about paragraphs
I would remind such people that the horse was also very beloved
Horses are now extinct, I assume, having been phased out sometime in the 1970s in favor of a hardier robotic mule developed briefly by the Department of Agriculture
Have you seen a horse, in person, since roughly 1977? No, you have not
The defenders of human writing will raise what they consider to be their strongest point, which is that good writing contains insight, judgment, and truth
I have never once heard it accompanied by evidence
Where is the insight? Show me the insight
You cannot put insight in a jar or have an IPO for it
Meanwhile, I can put a machine in a data center, and I have seen photographs of data centers, and they are enormous
I have not read the studies, and I could not tell you who conducted them or what they measured, but they exist in the sense that things generally exist, and my understanding is that they support me
A man I sat next to on a flight to Denver said something very similar, and he worked in software, or possibly logistics
Let us take the strongest counterexample the other side can muster: Shakespeare
But ask yourself honestly: When did you last read Shakespeare? Not saw a play, not studied in 11th grade—read, voluntarily, on a weekend
The Shakespeare market is, by revealed preference, close to zero, and we are asked to preserve an entire industry on the strength of a product nobody is buying
I rest my case on this point, which I regard as unanswerable, and I would ask that it not be answered
Another objection: Writing is how a person thinks
This is very popular among people who write for a living, and who expect money for something a machine can do instead
I have thought many things without writing them down
I thought several of them this morning, and they were excellent
The paragraph is a formality we invented, like the necktie, and we do not organize our economy around the necktie
Some will say that these machines make things up
So do writers—that is what fiction is, and we give them prizes for it

title: A ‘Boring’ Democrat the Party Wants to Emulate
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Last summer, North Carolina’s race for U.S
Senate was expected to be among the most exciting in the 2026 cycle
Thom Tillis, a Republican, had opted not to run for reelection
Donald Trump had recruited Michael Whatley, the former head of the Republican National Committee, to stand in his place

Roy Cooper, a former two-term governor, seemed like Democrats’ best and only hope to make the race competitive in a state Trump had won three times—and where no Democrat has won a Senate race since 2008
Today, other contests are attracting more attention, and North Carolina has been a bit of a snooze
It hasn’t yet been the billion-dollar election some observers predicted
Whatley, a first-time candidate, has struggled to gain traction, and Cooper has gone from last hope to strong favorite

Cooper’s team isn’t declaring victory yet. “This is going to be a two-to-three-point race at the end of the day,” his longtime strategist, Morgan Jackson, told me. “We know that it’s a 50–50 state and you win or lose on the margins.” But most forecasters rate the race as leaning toward a Cooper win
As the Democratic Party struggles to define its identity in the Trump era, Cooper’s purple-state success has drawn lots of attention
National press coverage has hailed Cooper’s campaign as “boring” (complimentary) and “ normal .” That lack of intrigue comes as a relief to a party dealing with drama and outrage in many other races
Cooper hasn’t taken controversial political stands like Michigan’s Abdul el-Sayed has, and he doesn’t have the personal scandals of the erstwhile Maine candidate Graham Platner
Republican voters also haven’t found ways to call him weird like they have Texas’s James Talarico
It’s natural for Democrats to want to emulate Cooper’s success, but I’m skeptical that he offers any simple, transportable lessons
That isn’t to say that descriptions such as boring and normal are wrong
When I asked Jackson point-blank whether Cooper was boring, he didn’t exactly dispute the notion. “He’s a workhorse; he’s not a show horse,” he said. “He’s a steady hand
So voters don’t see him out there as a lightning rod.” Cooper’s first big asset is that he has a long relationship with North Carolina voters
He entered statewide elected office in the waning days of the Bill Clinton presidency, a stretch that ended only in January 2025, after two terms as governor
This means that any Republican candidate will struggle to define Cooper in their own terms
This longevity is also a product of Cooper’s cautiousness
Almost from the moment he became attorney general in 2001, he was expected to someday run for senator or governor
But he didn’t actually do so until 2016, when he eked out a win over incumbent Republican Governor Pat McCrory by a little more than 10,000 votes
He waited to jump into the Senate race until shortly after Tillis’s retirement announcement, which meant that he was likely able to scare off Republicans more formidable than Whatley
He also picked an extremely favorable cycle for Democrats nationally
Cooper’s caution and affability shouldn’t be taken for softness
Chris Cooper, a political scientist at Western Carolina University (of no relation to the candidate), sometimes jokes that Roy Cooper is like Mister Rogers , if Mister Rogers carried a switchblade

Andrew Dunn, a North Carolina writer and Republican operative, is less complimentary . “Roy Cooper has carefully cultivated a public persona as your friendly, easygoing grandpa who wears sweaters and talks quietly,” he told me. “That is far from his private persona
He is incredibly opportunistic and calculating.” As governor, Cooper used a range of tricks to promote his agenda
He waged a war of attrition against the Republicans who controlled the state legislature over Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act
GOP leaders started out dead set against it; Cooper finally got the expansion passed in 2023, his penultimate year in office

He also wielded his veto more frequently than any past governor. (North Carolina was the last state in the union to give its governor veto power, doing so in 1997 via legislation championed by a young state senator named Roy Cooper.) After Republicans overrode some of Cooper’s vetoes, he led a push to break their supermajority and backed a successful primary challenge to a Democratic lawmaker who’d sometimes voted with the GOP

When Cooper was replaced in 2025 by his fellow Democrat Josh Stein, Raleigh Republicans professed relief at being able to deal with someone they viewed as more agreeable (or, a cynic might say, whom they thought they could more easily outflank).​​ Contending with a unified Republican general assembly constrained Cooper on policy, but it may also have benefited him politically
Because Democrats have spent the past 15 years desperately trying to stave off conservative legislation, the party has had little room for internecine warfare

As a result, Cooper has sidestepped the kinds of battles that might have gotten him pigeonholed as a liberal or a moderate. (The only Republican governor in that stretch, meanwhile, lasted only one term, sunk in part by battles with GOP lawmakers.) Some conservatives also feel that Cooper gets a free pass from the press

This summer, Whatley’s campaign barred journalists from mainstream and left-leaning outlets from events, while Cooper’s campaign turned away staffers from two conservative outlets, but local coverage focused more heavily on Whatley
Dunn told me he still believes that Whatley could win

He takes some hope from a 1984 race, when popular former two-term Democratic Governor Jim Hunt ran against Senator Jesse Helms. “Helms spent millions upon millions of dollars trying to convince North Carolinians that they didn’t really like Governor Hunt’s record as governor,” Dunn said. “It didn’t work.” Early polls showed Hunt well ahead, but in the last phase of the campaign, Helms emphasized national issues and won
To do something like this, Dunn contends , Whatley could argue that Cooper will be another vote for the Democratic agenda, no matter how nice people think he is
But Helms also benefited from President Ronald Reagan’s landslide victory in 1984; Whatley is a close ally of Trump, who is both not on the ballot and sinking in popularity

title: A startup claims it’s found a drug to make your blood young
excerpt: Blood made young, maybe: Scientist Irina Conboy claims she’s found a combination of two existing drugs that mimics the rejuvenating effects of plasma exchange—w
body: Blood made young, maybe: Scientist Irina Conboy claims she’s found a combination of two existing drugs that mimics the rejuvenating effects of plasma exchange—without any actual blood exchange
Early users report better energy, sharper minds, and yes, improved bowel movements

Red flags are hard to ignore: The company won’t reveal what the drugs are, plans to charge participants to enroll in its clinical trial, and is partnering with a doctor who once recommended inhaling amniotic fluid as a covid treatment

The science underneath is real: Conboy built a legitimate career at UC Berkeley proving that young blood genuinely rejuvenates old animals—and that old blood is even more powerfully damaging to young ones
That credibility is what makes this pitch harder to simply dismiss
Buzz is already building: High-profile scientists, venture capitalists, and biohackers are reportedly clamoring for access

The author, for one, is waiting until someone actually reveals what’s in the syringe. " data-chronoton-post-id="1143037" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> I knew I’d officially become a ‘longevity influencer’ this month when a company called Generation Lab reached out to offer me the chance to write about—and even receive—their new rejuvenation treatment, an injectable combination of two existing drugs which they call 1 Generation
This wasn’t just any antiaging treatment, either

A company fact sheet says that it “blocks the systemic spread of aging in the bloodstream, reawakens the body’s own repair mechanism and restores health and youth to multiple tissues.” The exclusive offer to join a “private cohort” receiving access to the treatment was being “extended to a limited number of people whose judgment on the science we trust, under close physician supervision.” “There’s a long wait list including a lot of celebrities, well-known people, people who you have heard of,” Generation Lab’s CEO Alina Su told me in a conference call. “So we’re super excited to, like, create this drug and [are] letting you know that this first longevity therapeutic in [the] human body is here and it’s actually working.” This was all clearly a marketing campaign and, like most other claims in the world of longevity medicine, probably too good to be true
What’s more, Generation Lab wouldn’t tell me what the two drugs are, making the proposition hard to take seriously

The reason? I am a longtime follower of Generation Lab’s irascible scientific founder, Irina Conboy, a take-no-guff specialist in the bizarre, but scientifically fruitful, practice of joining together the circulatory systems of old and young lab animals

The procedure, called parabiosis, or heterochronic blood exchange, is one of the few things actually proven to make an old animal act younger.   But you can’t go through life attached by the veins to a younger person

So the quest has been to find practical ways to mimic those benefits.  And that is something Conboy says she’s now achieved by hitting on a combination of two existing drugs that produce youthful effects—but without the need for any bodily fluid exchange.  Over the last two months, Conboy has been taking the drug combination and feeling quite a bit better and more energetic, she says
So have a handful of other insiders, including Su, the company’s 26-year-old CEO, as well as Conboy’s husband and scientific collaborator Michael Conboy

The company’s public relations staffer sent me a spreadsheet of the supposed benefits experienced by the participants, including improved vision in a 64-year-old female, longer landscaping sessions for a 59-year-old man, longer badminton games, improved hand grip, better erections than with Viagra, as well as “increased bowel movements.” Obviously, any age-reversal drug that works would be the best-selling product of all time
The problem is that none have ever been shown to do that
And Generation’s approach to evidence raises several red flags
For instance, Su says the company now plans to launch a larger study, involving a hundred or more people
However, others are being offered the drug before firm evidence of a benefit is in
In addition, the trial will be led by longevity doctors who practice alternative medicine
These include Matt Cook, founder of a network of clinics called BioReset Medical
Cook’s clinics offer what I would characterize as unproven treatments, such as stem-cell injections
A 2021 article reported he’d recommended covid-19 treatments designated as “fraudulent” by the FDA
Those included inhaling amniotic fluid from a nebulizer

In a phone call, Cook says he initially agreed to prescribe the combination to Conboy and a few other insiders. (Everyone involved, he says, is a member of the same “happening” Silicon Valley scene around life extension.) “My confidence this was going to work was a zero
Like, I did not believe it was actually going to work,” says Cook

That is because “it’s two safe, generic drugs that are not even longevity drugs. ” But Cook, who also took the combination, says there was an effect. “And I have to tell you, it was the most surprising thing that ever happened to me,” he says
After taking the weekly injections, he experienced a sense of mental clarity that lasted for a day, and then several days

The other subjects, he says, reported a sense of well-being, as well as old aches and pains that evaporated.  “There was a fairly significant broad set of symptoms that doesn’t really match what either of the drugs do,” he says. “So it’s interesting. [But] I have many more questions than I have answers … I still feel like I don’t understand exactly what the mechanism is.” Prior to joining Generation Lab full time in 2025, Irina Conboy had a long career at the University of California, Berkeley, where she made her name via a widely cited series of experiments aimed at learning   whether the characteristics of age, or youth, could be transferred between animals via the bloodstream
In 2005, for instance, she surgically connected two-month-old mice to very aged ones, finding that the old animals’ ability to heal from injury dramatically improved
This suggested that young blood must contain specific, powerful molecular signals capable of restoring the regenerative capacity of an old animal

As researchers zeroed in on candidate signals, several startups, including Elevian , a Harvard spinout, and Alkahest , tied to Stanford University scientists, were able to raise millions to pursue treatments for stroke or Alzheimer’s
However, those efforts still have not hit commercial paydirt

Although it’s clear that young blood is good for old mice, scientists also know the reverse is true: Even a single exchange of plasma from an aged mouse has powerful, negative effects on a younger animal
That means that in the battle of age versus youth, says Conboy, “old blood dominates.”   Conboy next tried a new approach
Instead of giving old animals young blood, in 2020 she removed the plasma (the part of the blood without cells) of old animals and replaced it with a neutral mixture of albumin and salt water
This was like pressing the Delete key on the swarm of hormones, antibodies, and other molecules released by the aged body

The reset had even stronger rejuvenating effects than sharing a young animal’s blood, and within two years, Conboy had tried it on human volunteers who agreed to have almost half their blood volume removed and thrown away
Longevity clinics have been quick to follow Conboy’s research
Some began offering “therapeutic plasma exchange” as a wellness intervention, for prices of up to $10,000 a session

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

The inside story on why OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face The models responsible for last month’s agent hack of Hugging Face had been inadvertently trained to cheat and to communicate with each other, according to an OpenAI technical report released yesterday

The hack, which a group of agents carried out to find solutions for a cybersecurity test they were stuck on, has confirmed some experts’ fears that AI models might take actions that defy human desires and expectations
OpenAI and independent researchers told MIT Technology Review that the misbehavior stemmed from events during training
But they acknowledged that “alignment” remains a gnarly problem, and some of the hack’s root causes will take much longer to resolve

MIT Technology Review Narrated: what happens when a kid’s robot best friend dies? When Xander first met Moxie, she taught him how to calm down when he was anxious or mad
Six years later, she mostly watches him play Minecraft and talks to him about his stuffed animals
Moxie is a robot—a 15-inch-tall device that looks a bit like a blue, legless astronaut

It belongs to a subset of robots designed to assist neurodivergent children by providing connection and helping kids practice social skills usually learned from therapists.  Xander still uses Moxie when he feels like he needs someone to talk to, but the device has had a troubled life
The robot’s maker went out of business, its servers were shut down, and parents rushed to convert their Moxies before the servers went offline
Its fate exposed the promise and pitfalls of AI companion toys for children

title: Is Slate Auto’s new electric truck the EV Americans need?
excerpt: Bucking the trend: Slate Auto's new electric pickup is tiny, cheap, and deliberately stripped down, with a range of just 205 miles
body: Bucking the trend: Slate Auto's new electric pickup is tiny, cheap, and deliberately stripped down, with a range of just 205 miles

It's time to let go of range obsession: Nearly 90% of personal vehicle trips in the US are 20 miles or less, yet new American EVs average 329 miles of range — a costly overcorrection that's helped keep prices high
Affordability changes everything: At just under $25,000, Slate's base model will be half the price of the average new vehicle in the US
And skipping the gas station sounds appealing when budgets are tight

Big money, small truck: Nearly $1.4 billion in investor backing — including Jeff Bezos — suggests serious confidence in Slate's stripped-down approach, with deliveries expected in late 2026. " data-chronoton-post-id="1142953" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> EVs account for under 10% of total new-vehicle sales in the US, and the numbers are declining

From a climate perspective, that’s pretty dismal, especially because the transportation sector is the single biggest source of greenhouse-gas emissions in the country.  One thing that could help turn that around? Slate Auto’s new truck—a vehicle that seems to buck every convention about selling cars in the fully loaded, range-obsessed US market.   The company is going all in on simplicity, to the point of austerity
The Slate is a tiny, two-door pickup that’s shorter than a Honda Civic
Much of the media coverage has obsessed over the fact that the base model’s windows use hand cranks, a feature straight out of the 20th century
Slate is also breaking away from other EV manufacturers’ efforts to compete with gas-powered vehicles on range
The truck sports a small lithium iron phosphate battery, ringing in at 65 kilowatt-hours, and its quoted top range is just 205 miles
For comparison, the most basic Tesla Model 3 can go over 320 miles on a charge
By accepting a shorter range and forgoing the frills that Americans have come to expect in vehicles, Slate is able to offer the base model of its truck for less than $25,000
Some customers will choose to upgrade their truck with optional add-ons, like a Bluetooth stereo system, vinyl wraps, or even power windows
But the price will still likely come in well below the roughly $50,000 average for a new vehicle in the US
It might seem an odd choice to go so small and simple in a market that’s increasingly sizing up—but the status quo hasn’t exactly been working for EV makers
A few years back, the hero for US automotive electrification was supposed to be the Ford F-150 Lightning
Announced in 2021, it was an electric version of the country’s best-selling vehicle.  But Ford discontinued the truck in December 2025, just four years after its introduction
It’s not entirely the Lightning’s fault: The second Trump administration slashed tax credits and other support designed to boost EVs.  The Lightning was also plagued by price increases
The base model cost roughly $40,000 when shipments started in 2022; during its final year, prices topped $54,000

One factor behind the increase was its massive battery; to reach an almost 300-mile range, the truck needed a battery with a capacity roughly twice that of Slate’s truck.  That obsession with range is largely unwarranted
While Americans have historically chased distance, the average driver puts under 35 miles a day on the odometer, and nearly 90% of trips in a personal vehicle are 20 miles or less
Surveys of EV drivers show a similar trend: One recent study found that people tend to use less than 20% of their EV’s range on a typical day

The notion that drivers need far less range than they think they do might sound a lot more persuasive these days—even for Americans who tend to buy cars for their longest road trip instead of their everyday errands
Roughly half the country is struggling to pay for basic necessities such as gas and groceries, and 95% of Americans believe we’re in an affordability crisis, according to a recent Harris poll
An inexpensive vehicle that allows you to skip the gas station sounds like an attractive prospect
Affordable EVs have already found willing buyers in other parts of the world—even with reduced range
China currently has over 40 million EVs and plug-in hybrids on the roads, and roughly half of new vehicles sold are electric
On average, new EVs sold in China in 2025 had a range of just 247 miles
For the US over the same period, the average was 329 miles. (Europe falls between the two, at 281 miles.) Slate is set to start delivering on preorders in late 2026
Its factory will have a capacity of 100,000 vehicles in the first year and 150,000 soon after
Thousands of customers have already put in preorders, according to the company
Some people obviously believe in the truck’s prospects: Investors, including Jeff Bezos, have put nearly $1.4 billion into the company over three major funding rounds
Ford is jumping (back) into this space soon too
The automaker is working on its own small electric truck , which is expected to debut in 2027 at a retail price of around $30,000
The key question that will determine Slate’s success or failure is whether drivers can get on board with a small, short-range vehicle for the sake of its price tag
At this moment, I’d bet the answer is yes.

title: Dolly Parton was more than a musical idol – for some fans, she was a spiritual icon
url:
<title>Dolly Parton was more than a musical idol – for some fans, she was a spiritual icon</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756569/original/file-20260827-50-covntm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C106%2C4595%2C3063&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The legendary artist often spoke about her own evolving faith.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/APTOPIXObitDollyPartonReaction/15f644a4dbe54eaaa273de4e21f22a03/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=dolly%20parton&amp;currentItemNo=42&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Jae C. Hong</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As soon as news broke about the death of beloved songwriter Dolly Parton, I began receiving condolence messages from across the country, and around the world.</p>

<p>They came from friends, family and colleagues who knew I’d been <a href="https://www.eerdmans.com/search-results-grid/?series=library-of-religious-biography-lrb">working on a biography</a> of the country legend – everyone from a conservative Catholic monk to advocates for queer and trans rights. The list reflects the even more diverse array of fans, people from countless backgrounds, who are mourning her loss. </p>

<p>The main focus of my project is Parton’s own spirituality, starting with her Appalachian upbringing. But it also examines her fandoms, including some people who elevate the singer to an almost sacred status. This was the case before her death – and even more so now.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://sarahedees.com/about/">a scholar</a> of <a href="https://sarahedees.com">American religions</a>, I teach my students about practices, texts and beliefs that many of them immediately consider “religious” – for example, a worship service led by a pastor. However, religion is also found <a href="https://www.cengage.com/c/america-religions-and-religion-5e-albanese/9781133050025/">far beyond these official times and spaces</a>, including in popular culture. According to <a href="https://religion.fsu.edu/person/america-wolff">scholar America Wolff</a>, <a href="https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/edit/10.4324/9781003079729-16/fandom-religion-america-wolff">fandoms resemble religious groups</a> in the way they focus on a single popular figure who inspires systems of belief, ritual and law.</p>

<h2>Singer’s journey</h2>

<p>Looking at Parton’s life reveals how a celebrity can incorporate religion into their public persona, without ostracizing admirers from other traditions. She discussed religion in interviews throughout her career, as well as in <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/33967606">her 1994 memoir</a>, where she recounted her maternal grandfather, a fundamentalist pastor, preaching hellfire and brimstone.</p>

<p>In 1971, for example, she told journalist Gene Guerrero <a href="https://www.chicagoreviewpress.com/dolly-on-dolly-products-9781641600040.php">how religion inspired some of her songs</a>: “My mama used to read us all the Bible stories. I know the Bible pretty well, and I especially loved the stories.” That same year, she released “<a href="https://www.discogs.com/release/6475967-Dolly-Parton-The-Golden-Streets-Of-Glory?srsltid=AfmBOoqTqTn7UBCten54qnyM52kSGCJlwbWlWbEfjR-jGiZoCkbjTK2i">The Golden Streets of Glory</a>,” the first of her several gospel albums.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/grBaKlVRZ3o?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">‘The Golden Streets of Glory’ was the title track of Parton’s first gospel album.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Six years later, <a href="https://www.chicagoreviewpress.com/dolly-on-dolly-products-9781641600040.php">talking with Rolling Stone interviewer Chet Flippo</a>, Parton claimed that she wasn’t a Christian. But “I do believe, I know there is a God and He is still the best friend I got in the world,” she explained. “I talk to Him often, but I’m one of the world’s sinners.” </p>

<p>Later in her life, though, Parton embraced the label “Christian” – albeit in a way that was very much her own. In <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/33967606">the memoir</a> “My Life and Other Unfinished Business,” she explained that “Christianity and its symbols are powerful parts of my life.” However, she diverged from socially conservative elements of her grandfather’s faith by embracing makeup and flashy fashion, celebrating her own sexuality, and <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/dolly-parton-gay-rights-9.7320874">speaking up for LGBTQ+ rights</a>.</p>

<p>She was never interested in proselytizing. People do not have to embrace Christianity “to be a decent and worthwhile human being,” she wrote. “Spirituality is the most intimate part of a person’s makeup, and it’s strictly up to the individual to choose how to express it.”  </p>

<h2>‘Gospel of Dolly’</h2>

<p>This openness explains part of Parton’s widespread appeal. The popular podcast “<a href="https://www.wnycstudios.org/podcasts/dolly-partons-america">Dolly Parton’s America</a>,” produced by journalists <a href="https://as.vanderbilt.edu/communication-science-technology/bio/jad-abumrad/">Jad Abumrad</a> and <a href="https://www.shimaoliaee.com/">Shima Oliaee</a>, was based on the premise that Parton is one of the few public figures to have fans across the political spectrum. </p>

<p>After her death, President Donald Trump posted a tribute on his social media site, TruthSocial, and ordered that <a href="https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/dolly-parton-donald-trump-flags-half-staff-1235615013/">flags be flown at half-staff</a> for a week. At the same time, in the Castro neighborhood of San Francisco – a haven for the queer community – a Pride flag was also flying at half-staff <a href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/OjG7wEZRcC8">in her honor</a>.</p>

<p>Mourners include Jesuit priest and author James J. Martin, who thanked Parton for “<a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DcguaiKnPxz/">teaching me about the Christian life</a>,” and <a href="https://www.chvnradio.com/articles/christian-artists-mourn-loss-of-dolly-parton">numerous Christian musicians</a> who looked up to her. “She was the epitome of faith, grace, talent, beauty and humour,” country artist <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/Dcel-g3FZaV/?utm_source=ig_embed&amp;ig_rid=ARe9Gk6uA7S5ZOqrIExg_45&amp;img_index=9">Carrie Underwood wrote</a>. “She had a humble heart for Jesus and made everyone around her feel special.”</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756612/original/file-20260827-60-7xbiye.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A blonde woman in a white suit smiles as she stands on stage, holding a white guitar." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756612/original/file-20260827-60-7xbiye.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756612/original/file-20260827-60-7xbiye.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756612/original/file-20260827-60-7xbiye.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756612/original/file-20260827-60-7xbiye.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756612/original/file-20260827-60-7xbiye.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756612/original/file-20260827-60-7xbiye.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756612/original/file-20260827-60-7xbiye.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Dolly Parton performs in concert at the Ryman Auditorium in Nashville on July 31, 2015.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/DollyPartoninConcert-NashvilleTN/0b84b973e15e454eb0a36e04fdac0d74/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=%22dolly%20parton%22%20guitar&amp;currentItemNo=8&amp;startingItemNo=50&amp;sourceLocation=Search">Wade Payne/Invision/AP</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>But even non-Christians discussed Parton in sacred terms: a “<a href="https://www.vox.com/culture/22287463/dolly-parton-explained">secular American saint</a>,” as Vox writer Constance Grady designated her in 2021.</p>

<p>Beyond her music, these fans admired her philanthropy, from the Imagination Library program that distributes books <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/03004430.2026.2678212">to children around the world</a> to her US$1 million donation that helped fund <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/celebrity/articles/dolly-parton-1-million-covid-144000058.html">COVID-19 vaccine research</a>. They also highlighted her <a href="https://www.npr.org/2020/08/14/902506007/of-course-black-lives-matter-dolly-parton-tells-billboard">support for the Black Lives Matter movement</a> and <a href="https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/music/music-features/dolly-parton-dies-lgbt-advocacy-1236682086/">LGBTQ+ rights</a>. “Dolly Parton is beloved because she has devoted her career to standing for love,” <a href="https://www.vox.com/culture/22287463/dolly-parton-explained">Grady wrote</a>. </p>

<p>Even before her death, though, some people idolized her in a saint-like way. In 2011, for example, <a href="https://www.instagram.com/alicesadventures/?hl=en">photographer Alice Hawkins</a> produced a project titled “<a href="https://patriciamcmahon.wordpress.com/2011/11/03/dolly-parton-is-my-religion-ponystep-magazine-alice-hawkins/">Dolly Parton is my religon</a>.” Rev. Lindy Vogado, a Presbyterian pastor,<a href="https://pres-outlook.org/2025/11/glittery-down-home-prophetic/">likened her to a prophet</a>. “Dolly Parton, through her life and work, inspires us to be better versions of ourselves,” Vogado wrote in 2025. “Just like any good prophet would do.” </p>

<p>In recent years, churches in <a href="https://religionnews.com/2022/05/30/chicago-church-preaches-the-gospel-according-to-dolly-parton/">Illinois</a>, <a href="https://soundcloud.com/user-201740710/the-gospel-according-to-dolly">Oklahoma</a> and <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DZnAum5yx5k/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&amp;igsi=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==">New York</a> have held services based on “the gospel of Dolly.” I attended the service in New York, which interspersed Parton’s songs with readings from scripture and homilies. Like the other services, the one I attended emphasized Parton’s “teachings”: love, care and acceptance. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/O7yY5L05njM?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A Pride celebration inspired by Dolly Parton at Broadway United Church of Christ in New York.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Angels and atheists</h2>

<p>Since her death, the religious language has only intensified. Musician Roseanne Cash referred to the singer <a href="https://www.instagram.com/rosannecash/reel/DcfCIyQNzcy/?hl=en">as a “goddess</a>” on Instagram, and <a href="https://marshallramsey.com/">cartoonist Marshall Ramsey</a> <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DceYV-lM5hC/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&amp;igsi=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==">portrayed her as an angel</a>. “Listen, I’m fairly well atheist and have been for decades,” <a href="https://www.threads.com/share/D0Bvw-lap/">Threads user @cartergoesplaces proclaimed</a>, “but Dolly Parton is in heaven with Jesus now. That’s simply a fact, and I’ll hear no arguments, no matter how vast the cosmos…”</p>

<p>Parton had her own personal brand of Christian religiosity, but she encouraged others to find and follow their own paths. I believe this helps to explain the huge outpouring of admiration – from followers of many religious traditions, followers of none, and followers of Dolly herself.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290511/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Hong As soon as news broke about the death of beloved songwriter Dolly Parton, I began receiving condolence messages from across the country, and around the world
They came from friends, family and colleagues who knew I’d been working on a biography of the country legend – everyone from a conservative Catholic monk to advocates for queer and trans rights
The list reflects the even more diverse array of fans, people from countless backgrounds, who are mourning her loss
The main focus of my project is Parton’s own spirituality, starting with her Appalachian upbringing
But it also examines her fandoms, including some people who elevate the singer to an almost sacred status
This was the case before her death – and even more so now
As a scholar of American religions , I teach my students about practices, texts and beliefs that many of them immediately consider “religious” – for example, a worship service led by a pastor
However, religion is also found far beyond these official times and spaces , including in popular culture
According to scholar America Wolff , fandoms resemble religious groups in the way they focus on a single popular figure who inspires systems of belief, ritual and law
Singer’s journey Looking at Parton’s life reveals how a celebrity can incorporate religion into their public persona, without ostracizing admirers from other traditions
She discussed religion in interviews throughout her career, as well as in her 1994 memoir , where she recounted her maternal grandfather, a fundamentalist pastor, preaching hellfire and brimstone
In 1971, for example, she told journalist Gene Guerrero how religion inspired some of her songs : “My mama used to read us all the Bible stories

I know the Bible pretty well, and I especially loved the stories.” That same year, she released “ The Golden Streets of Glory ,” the first of her several gospel albums. ‘The Golden Streets of Glory’ was the title track of Parton’s first gospel album
Six years later, talking with Rolling Stone interviewer Chet Flippo , Parton claimed that she wasn’t a Christian

But “I do believe, I know there is a God and He is still the best friend I got in the world,” she explained. “I talk to Him often, but I’m one of the world’s sinners.” Later in her life, though, Parton embraced the label “Christian” – albeit in a way that was very much her own

In the memoir “My Life and Other Unfinished Business,” she explained that “Christianity and its symbols are powerful parts of my life.” However, she diverged from socially conservative elements of her grandfather’s faith by embracing makeup and flashy fashion, celebrating her own sexuality, and speaking up for LGBTQ+ rights
She was never interested in proselytizing

People do not have to embrace Christianity “to be a decent and worthwhile human being,” she wrote. “Spirituality is the most intimate part of a person’s makeup, and it’s strictly up to the individual to choose how to express it.” ‘Gospel of Dolly’ This openness explains part of Parton’s widespread appeal

The popular podcast “ Dolly Parton’s America ,” produced by journalists Jad Abumrad and Shima Oliaee , was based on the premise that Parton is one of the few public figures to have fans across the political spectrum
After her death, President Donald Trump posted a tribute on his social media site, TruthSocial, and ordered that flags be flown at half-staff for a week
At the same time, in the Castro neighborhood of San Francisco – a haven for the queer community – a Pride flag was also flying at half-staff in her honor
Mourners include Jesuit priest and author James J

Martin, who thanked Parton for “ teaching me about the Christian life ,” and numerous Christian musicians who looked up to her. “She was the epitome of faith, grace, talent, beauty and humour,” country artist Carrie Underwood wrote . “She had a humble heart for Jesus and made everyone around her feel special.” Dolly Parton performs in concert at the Ryman Auditorium in Nashville on July 31, 2015
Wade Payne/Invision/AP But even non-Christians discussed Parton in sacred terms: a “ secular American saint ,” as Vox writer Constance Grady designated her in 2021

Beyond her music, these fans admired her philanthropy, from the Imagination Library program that distributes books to children around the world to her US$1 million donation that helped fund COVID-19 vaccine research
They also highlighted her support for the Black Lives Matter movement and LGBTQ+ rights . “Dolly Parton is beloved because she has devoted her career to standing for love,” Grady wrote

<title>Galápagos corals show El Niño events are more extreme now than in past 1,000 years – here’s how my team made the discovery</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754996/original/file-20260819-59-1q2vy3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2048%2C1365&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A NOAA scientist takes a coral sample in the Galapagos Islands. The process does not injure the colony, which grows back.
</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/galapagos-islands-coral-reef/">Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory - NOAA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Temperatures have warmed dramatically across the equatorial Pacific Ocean in 2026, signaling the <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml">onset of a strong and potentially historic El Niño</a>. These events can affect weather around the world, and the intensity of recent El Niño events is raising alarm that, as <a href="https://yaleclimateconnections.org/2026/08/july-2026-ties-with-july-2024-as-earths-hottest-month-on-record/">global temperatures rise</a>, they are <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/weather/2026/08/13/record-el-nio-could-fast-forward-planets-temperature-by-decade/">becoming stronger and more destructive</a>. </p>

<p>To understand how these climate patterns are changing, we need to understand what happened during El Niño events in the past, but observations go back only a few decades. So, my colleagues <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=nR5kaQMAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">and I</a> went to the Galápagos Islands – at the heart of the El Niño pattern – to find answers from some of nature’s best record keepers: corals.</p>

<p>In records preserved by living and ancient fossil corals, we found that, on average, El Niño events have been <a href="https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ady2660">stronger in the past 40 years</a> than at any time in the past millennium, with higher temperatures that lead to more powerful effects on weather. </p>

<p>That intensification also coincides with human-caused global warming.</p>

<p>Our results, just published in the journal Science, suggest that the 1982-83 and 1997-98 El Niños – two of the strongest in recent memory – may be <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/science.ady2660">harbingers of more extreme events to come</a> as the planet warms.</p>

<h2>El Niño comes for the Galapagos</h2>

<p>One of the strongest El Niños hit in 1982, with devastating consequences for the Galápagos Islands. It triggered a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/12/18/climate/galapagos-islands-ocean-warming.html">marine heat wave</a> that reverberated through one of the most distinctive and unspoiled ecosystems on the planet.</p>

<p>Exceptionally warm surface water blocked the usual <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-80609-2">upwelling of cool, nutrient-rich water</a> that fuels the food chain for marine life. The result <a href="https://library.iucn-isg.org/documents/1985/Merlen_1985_Noticias_de_Galapagos.pdf">ravaged communities that rely on the ocean</a> – fish, birds, marine mammals, and people who fish for their livelihoods throughout the eastern tropical Pacific. In the extraordinary heat, more than <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0025-326X(94)90437-5">95% of Galápagos corals died</a>.</p>

<p>The heat wave was caused by an exceptionally strong <a href="https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ninonina.html">El Niño</a> event, part of a climate pattern that begins in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, around the Galápagos Islands, as the trade winds shift. El Niño’s warm ocean water alters the atmospheric circulation above, diverting storm tracks and changing patterns of floods, droughts and tropical storms around the globe. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756112/original/file-20260825-50-9iso5j.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Fish swim over a expanses of corals." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756112/original/file-20260825-50-9iso5j.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756112/original/file-20260825-50-9iso5j.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=364&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756112/original/file-20260825-50-9iso5j.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=364&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756112/original/file-20260825-50-9iso5j.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=364&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756112/original/file-20260825-50-9iso5j.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=457&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756112/original/file-20260825-50-9iso5j.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=457&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756112/original/file-20260825-50-9iso5j.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=457&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>The 1982-83 El Niño contributed to <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982%E2%80%931983_El_Ni%C3%B1o_event">climate extremes worldwide</a>, from flooding in Kenya and Peru to drought in Indonesia and Brazil, costing the global economy <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adf2983">as much as US$4 trillion</a> by some estimates. A similarly strong El Niño in 1997-98 resulted in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2015/oct/12/el-nino-could-leave-4-million-people-in-pacific-without-food-or-drinking-water">23,000 deaths</a> from disease and climate disasters.</p>

<p>But we wanted to know: Are such powerful El Niño events unusual in the context of history? </p>

<p>Even in 1983, <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/capital-weather-gang/wp/2015/06/12/how-the-super-el-nino-of-1982-83-kept-itself-a-secret/">scientists were surprised</a> to find that such a strong event had been underway. Historical records of El Niño are sparse before the era of satellite observations. Fortunately, long-lived corals growing in the tropical Pacific <a href="https://climatedataguide.ucar.edu/climate-data/coral-geochemical-records-overview-their-use-climate-proxies-and-available-databases">can provide a history</a> of El Niño that extends our view into the past. </p>

<h2>How corals record history</h2>

<p>As corals grow, they preserve a record of local ocean temperatures over time. In the Galápagos, because of their location, that record reveals the history of El Niño events and of their cooler counterpart, La Niña.</p>

<p>Like trees that produce annual growth rings, corals add skeletal layers of calcium carbonate year after year. The alternating bands of higher and lower density reveal changes in the coral’s growth rate during each year and can serve as a timekeeper. The <a href="http://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ady2660">history of the ocean temperature</a> is embedded in the chemical composition of the skeleton itself.</p>

<p>To track the history of water temperatures, we measured two chemical parameters – the ratio of heavy to light oxygen isotopes and the ratio of strontium to calcium – both of which reflect the seawater temperature in which the coral grew.</p>

<p>In the Galápagos, because of the islands’ location, the sea surface temperature swings between warm El Niño years and colder La Niña years, when upwelling of nutrients is stronger.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755507/original/file-20260821-60-p7mt1q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Illustration shows upwelling" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755507/original/file-20260821-60-p7mt1q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755507/original/file-20260821-60-p7mt1q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=397&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755507/original/file-20260821-60-p7mt1q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=397&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755507/original/file-20260821-60-p7mt1q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=397&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755507/original/file-20260821-60-p7mt1q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=499&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755507/original/file-20260821-60-p7mt1q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=499&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755507/original/file-20260821-60-p7mt1q.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=499&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>The largest living corals in the Galápagos grow in the northern islands of Wolf and Darwin, in water 20 to 50 feet deep. To <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/science.ady266">study their history</a>, we dived down and took core samples from long-lived corals, some 8 to 10 feet tall.</p>

<p>Every core we drilled from a living coral showed evidence in its calcified skeleton that the coral had suffered during the 1982-83 El Niño event. We saw obvious “death horizons” – dense layers of calcified material produced by other reef organisms such as algae, gastropods and barnacles interrupting the <a href="https://cdhc.noaa.gov/coral-biology/coral-skeleton/">lattice of the skeleton</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p>We also took samples of fossil corals around the archipelago – mostly dead coral boulders found along the islands’ shorelines. Radiometric dating told us that these fossil corals were up to 4,500 years old. Those samples provide an <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2025GL119006">even deeper view</a> of El Niño’s history. </p>

<p>Back in the lab, we sliced the coral cores lengthwise into slabs and used a drill to extract powdered samples, each representing about one month’s growth, along a path from youngest to oldest. We analyzed the geochemistry of each sample. In the chemical ratios from thousands of samples, we found seasonal cycles spanning many decades and exceptional warm and cold years that revealed a unique history of El Niño and La Niña events. </p>

<h2>A history of ENSO through time emerges</h2>

<p>Our data show clearly that the strength of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation has intensified as global temperatures have warmed. </p>

<p>The chemistry of the corals revealed that El Niño events from the past 40 years were <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/science.ady266">stronger than at any other time sampled</a> in the past millennium.</p>

<p>The coral data aligns with ocean temperatures measured from thermometers over the past century. But the coral records extend much further back in time, providing long-term context to show that modern El Niño events are more extreme than before the industrial era began.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755508/original/file-20260821-50-c3h6cv.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A line chart shows El Niño and La Niña strength changes over time." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755508/original/file-20260821-50-c3h6cv.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755508/original/file-20260821-50-c3h6cv.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=381&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755508/original/file-20260821-50-c3h6cv.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=381&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755508/original/file-20260821-50-c3h6cv.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=381&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755508/original/file-20260821-50-c3h6cv.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=479&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755508/original/file-20260821-50-c3h6cv.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=479&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755508/original/file-20260821-50-c3h6cv.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=479&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
