Triangles show results derived from the ratio of strontium to calcium, and circles show results from the ratio of oxygen isotopes. The red line indicates the global temperature estimated from other paleoclimate data. Coral data is plotted as the standard deviation of reconstructed Galápagos temperature on left axis, and global temperature data is plotted as deviations from the 1961-1990 average on the right axis.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Julia Cole</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The El Niño intensification we observed, starting in the mid- to late 20th century, is also greater than what nearly all climate models suggest would result from natural causes. It appears to be closely connected to human-caused global warming – a conclusion in line with expectations from <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s43017-023-00427-8">most climate models</a>. </p>

<p>Not all models <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/enso-and-climate-change-what-does-new-ipcc-report-say">anticipate El Niños strengthening</a> as the climate warms, but our data shows that unusual strengthening has accompanied recent warming – an association that may allow scientists to identify models that most closely track observations.</p>

<h2>Looking ahead</h2>

<p>A stronger El Niño-Southern Oscillation means more intense and damaging climate extremes across the globe. If humanity can anticipate those hazards, we can prepare and perhaps avoid the worst damage.</p>

<p>Fortunately, scientists understand enough about El Niño and La Niña events today to be able to <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/precip/CWlink/MJO/enso.shtml">forecast them up to a year in advance</a>. But such predictions depend on continuous, careful <a href="https://sealevel.jpl.nasa.gov/data/el-nino-la-nina-watch-and-pdo/overview/">climate measurements from satellites</a> and <a href="https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/gtmba/pmel-theme/pacific-ocean-tao">buoys across the remote tropical Pacific</a>, coupled with continuous improvements in <a href="https://www.gfdl.noaa.gov/climate-variability-and-prediction/">climate modeling and forecasting</a> capabilities. </p>

<p>Those capabilities are now more important than ever as global warming accelerates.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/272318/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory - NOAA Temperatures have warmed dramatically across the equatorial Pacific Ocean in 2026, signaling the onset of a strong and potentially historic El Niño
These events can affect weather around the world, and the intensity of recent El Niño events is raising alarm that, as global temperatures rise , they are becoming stronger and more destructive
To understand how these climate patterns are changing, we need to understand what happened during El Niño events in the past, but observations go back only a few decades
So, my colleagues and I went to the Galápagos Islands – at the heart of the El Niño pattern – to find answers from some of nature’s best record keepers: corals

In records preserved by living and ancient fossil corals, we found that, on average, El Niño events have been stronger in the past 40 years than at any time in the past millennium, with higher temperatures that lead to more powerful effects on weather
That intensification also coincides with human-caused global warming

Our results, just published in the journal Science, suggest that the 1982-83 and 1997-98 El Niños – two of the strongest in recent memory – may be harbingers of more extreme events to come as the planet warms
Our World in Data , CC BY El Niño comes for the Galapagos One of the strongest El Niños hit in 1982, with devastating consequences for the Galápagos Islands
It triggered a marine heat wave that reverberated through one of the most distinctive and unspoiled ecosystems on the planet
Exceptionally warm surface water blocked the usual upwelling of cool, nutrient-rich water that fuels the food chain for marine life
The result ravaged communities that rely on the ocean – fish, birds, marine mammals, and people who fish for their livelihoods throughout the eastern tropical Pacific
In the extraordinary heat, more than 95% of Galápagos corals died
The heat wave was caused by an exceptionally strong El Niño event, part of a climate pattern that begins in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, around the Galápagos Islands, as the trade winds shift
El Niño’s warm ocean water alters the atmospheric circulation above, diverting storm tracks and changing patterns of floods, droughts and tropical storms around the globe
The Galápagos Islands are known for their astounding marine biodiversity, a result of high nutrients and the mixing of cool and warm waters

Greg Asner/DivePhoto.org The 1982-83 El Niño contributed to climate extremes worldwide , from flooding in Kenya and Peru to drought in Indonesia and Brazil, costing the global economy as much as US$4 trillion by some estimates
A similarly strong El Niño in 1997-98 resulted in 23,000 deaths from disease and climate disasters
But we wanted to know: Are such powerful El Niño events unusual in the context of history? Even in 1983, scientists were surprised to find that such a strong event had been underway
Historical records of El Niño are sparse before the era of satellite observations
Fortunately, long-lived corals growing in the tropical Pacific can provide a history of El Niño that extends our view into the past
How corals record history As corals grow, they preserve a record of local ocean temperatures over time
In the Galápagos, because of their location, that record reveals the history of El Niño events and of their cooler counterpart, La Niña
Like trees that produce annual growth rings, corals add skeletal layers of calcium carbonate year after year
The alternating bands of higher and lower density reveal changes in the coral’s growth rate during each year and can serve as a timekeeper
The history of the ocean temperature is embedded in the chemical composition of the skeleton itself

To track the history of water temperatures, we measured two chemical parameters – the ratio of heavy to light oxygen isotopes and the ratio of strontium to calcium – both of which reflect the seawater temperature in which the coral grew

<title>US-Canada trade war deepens as Trump revives Depression-era trade tool – what’s at stake for consumers and the midterms</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756509/original/file-20260827-50-mt564g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=787%2C0%2C4405%2C2936&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">U.S. and Canadian flags wave in the wind next to Blue Water Bridge, which connects Port Huron, Mich., and Point Edward, Ontario.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/VirusOutbreakUSCanadaBorder/e51d6e322d6e457b9181348eec852df8/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=Blue%20Water%20Bridge&amp;currentItemNo=14&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Paul Sancya</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The United States and Canada, historically close allies, are moving further into a full-blown trade war with no end in sight.</p>

<p>On Aug. 25, 2026, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/08/25/us/trump-news-tariffs">Canada imposed tariffs of up to 50%</a> on hundreds of U.S. goods after the U.S. placed similar, <a href="https://tax.thomsonreuters.com/blog/section-338-tariffs-on-canada-what-businesses-may-be-missing-beyond-the-headline-categories/">long-threatened levies</a> on Canadian products. It followed the collapse of trade talks that had been inching towards a deal.</p>

<p>The next day, U.S. President Donald Trump <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=264OoaHKEUo">called Canada</a> “one of the worst countries in the world to deal with.” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/live/cmd94dl9pyqgt">claimed Trump</a> was trying to “destroy” his country’s auto industry. Only a few days earlier a deal <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/us-canada-trade-talks-collapse-as-new-50-tariffs-go-into-effect-160526827.html">was reportedly very close</a>.</p>

<p>One of the most notable aspects of the collapse in trade negotiations lies in Trump’s unprecedented use of an untested tool in the <a href="https://history.state.gov/milestones/1921-1936/protectionism">Tariff Act of 1930</a>,  otherwise known as the Smoot-Hawley tariffs. Economists generally agree that the act’s escalating retaliatory tariffs <a href="https://www.senate.gov/artandhistory/history/minute/Senate_Passes_Smoot_Hawley_Tariff.htm">extended the Great Depression</a> by sparking a global trade war. Amplified by foreign retaliation and falling global gross domestic product, U.S. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/ej/ueac006">trade fell by two-thirds</a> from 1929-1932.</p>

<p>Smoot-Hawley contains a provision known as Section 338, which provides an additional feature: The president may, on his own authority, impose unilateral tariffs of 50% if a foreign country’s policies “discriminated” against the United States.</p>

<p>But the section was never invoked, as the damage from the other Smoot-Hawley tariffs was already done. That is, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/business/trump-canada-tariffs.html">until July 2026</a>, when <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/07/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-imposes-additional-tariffs-on-canada/">Trump first threatened the 50% tariffs</a> on Canada for its “discriminatory treatment” of U.S. products.</p>

<p>As an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Lyq_bsgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">economist who has studied trade policy</a> for 49 years, I can explain how the two countries got embroiled in a trade war and what it means for U.S. consumers, companies and the midterms. </p>



<h2>Why did the trade deal collapse?</h2>

<p>Both sides are finger-pointing at the other over what caused the proposed deal to fall apart during the final days of the trade negotiations.</p>

<p>The Canadians <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/world/canada/trump-carney-trade-war-tariffs.html">were interested primarily</a> in reducing high U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos. They claimed they had a preliminary deal to lower steel and aluminum tariffs from 50% to 25%. </p>

<p>In the late stages of the negotiations, however, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6049271-lutnick-canada-trade-war-trump-tariffs/">was apparently lobbied heavily</a> by U.S. steel and aluminum producers to hold the line on these tariffs. Lutnick was also against reductions in the U.S. auto and truck tariffs and allegedly withdrew whatever reductions were on the table. </p>

<p>As a result, other parts of the deal started to unwind as well. </p>

<p>The Canadians had offered to reopen the <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/keystone-xl-expansion-timeline-9.7312229">Keystone oil pipeline deal</a> that had been canceled by President Joe Biden in 2021. But once the deal on lower steel, aluminum and auto tariffs was nixed, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/world/canada/trump-carney-trade-war-tariffs.html">Canada pulled the Keystone deal</a> off the table as well. </p>

<p>The U.S. <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/new-brunswick/no-return-us-booze-without-tariff-relief-9.7312951">had also demanded that Canada reverse</a> the Canadian provinces’ removal of U.S. liquor off their store shelves. <a href="https://theconversation.com/canada-is-kicking-its-us-booze-habit-as-trade-tensions-persist-279918">Sales of U.S. booze in Canada have plunged</a> as a result.</p>

<p>But the lack of progress on the major metal and auto tariffs, combined with a backlash from the Canadian provinces themselves, forced that concession off the table as well. </p>



<h2>What tariffs did the US place on Canadian goods?</h2>

<p>Canada is a <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF12595">major supplier of goods to the U.S.</a>, exporting about US$451 billion in 2025 – ranking second after Mexico.</p>

<p>As soon as talks broke off, the Trump administration <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/world/canada/carney-canada-trump-tariffs-retaliate.html">followed through on earlier threats</a> to impose a 50% tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian exports, including auto parts, forestry products, furniture, textiles, whiskey and hockey equipment, under Section 338 of Smoot-Hawley.</p>

<p>That’s about 4% of Canada’s exports to the United States. </p>

<h2>How did Canada retaliate?</h2>

<p>Canada’s Carney responded with his own already prepared list of $20 billion in U.S. imports to face tariffs of up to 50%, targeting products that he surely bets <a href="https://www.newsweek.com/map-shows-senate-battlegrounds-hit-hardest-by-canada-tariffs-12367218">will anger voters</a> in swing states heading into the midterm elections. </p>

<p>Examples include <a href="https://www.wsj.com/world/americas/canada-targets-u-s-metals-foods-motorcycles-in-retaliatory-tariff-package-f677222b?eafs_enabled=false">Wisconsin cheese, Maine seafood and Kentucky washers and dryers</a> – GE Appliances is headquartered in Louisville, Kentucky.</p>

<h2>How did two very close allies get into a trade war?</h2>

<p>Tensions between Canada and the U.S. and have been high ever since Trump returned to office.</p>

<p>He has continually complained about Canada “<a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/08/president-trump-is-finally-ending-canadas-free-ride/">ripping us off</a>” and being “<a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-calls-canada-worst-countries-deal-amid-ongoing/story?id=135973705">among the worst countries</a>” in the world to deal with. </p>

<p>And he has repeatedly <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cn4j38gk8edo">threatened to make Canada</a> the 51st state, an issue that has particularly angered Canadians and served to <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/26/world/canada/carney-canada-trump-tariffs-retaliate.html">unite public opinion</a> across the political spectrum against Trump.</p>

<p>For Carney, a critical sticking point was the late addition by U.S. negotiators requiring Canadian trade policy to align permanently with U.S. interests. <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/world/canada/trump-carney-trade-war-tariffs.html">Carney viewed this demand as a transfer of Canadian sovereignty</a> to the U.S., a step toward making Canada “the 51st state.” </p>

<p>So all in all, perhaps it’s not so surprising that a near deal would collapse into a trade war. </p>

<p>In addition, Canada has been unusual in standing up to Trump in this way. The only other country to do that is China, and it’s risky for a smaller country like Canada to retaliate in this way. But Canadians are pretty united in <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/24/canadians-opinions-of-the-us-and-its-president-are-at-or-near-historic-lows/">their unfavorable views of Trump</a>, so Carney has a strong domestic position to stand up to him.</p>

            </figcaption>

<h2>What does this mean for US consumers and businesses?</h2>

<p>The 50% tariffs Trump unilaterally imposed on Canada apply to goods that had previously been exempt from most other tariffs due to the <a href="https://ustr.gov/trade-agreements/free-trade-agreements/united-states-mexico-canada-agreement">United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement</a>, which replaced NAFTA in 2020.</p>

<p>Since <a href="https://theconversation.com/tariffs-101-what-they-are-who-pays-them-and-why-they-matter-now-271576">tariffs are a tax</a> on the purchaser, U.S. consumers and companies will have to pay 50% more to buy the products subject to the tariffs. Many of the Canadian imports are <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/trump-trade-war-canada-threatens-2026-republicans-border-states-rcna594137">concentrated in U.S. border states</a> such as Maine, New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio and Wisconsin. Another border state, Michigan, is closely tied to automobile production with the Canadian province of Ontario.</p>

<p>In many cases, Canada’s retaliatory tariffs will be felt most strongly in states where Trump’s Republican Party stands to be affected by reductions in U.S. exports that will result from the levies.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://time.com/article/2026/08/04/us-states-suing-trump-administration-tariffs-backlash/">political backlash</a> against Trump’s tariffs in the U.S. doesn’t appear to be deterring him from imposing more of them, even as the <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/how-trumps-trade-war-with-canada-could-rattle-states-with-key-senate-races">impact of midterm elections hinges</a> on results in several swing states along the Canadian border.</p>

<p>While the total impact on overall U.S. prices may not be large, the combination of U.S. and Canadian tariffs together could be significant for products that are heavily traded between the two countries, such as Michigan auto parts and New England seafood, as well as in U.S. regions where Canadian market shares are large. <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-us-canada-trade-war-could-change-how-american-farmers-grow-their-crops-for-years-290504">U.S farmers</a> and manufacturers may also lose sales to Canada.</p>

<p>If Trump’s tariffs remain in place and U.S. importers can no longer absorb the tariff costs and remain profitable, U.S. prices are likely to continue to rise as importers require consumers to pay a larger share of the tariffs. It’s probably unwise to predict what Trump will do with tariffs between now and the midterms or now and the end of his term in 2028. A victorious Democratic Party in charge of the House and Senate could change the political landscape considerably.</p>

<p>It’s worth noting that the global trading system that emerged in 1947, from the ashes of war, depression and tit-for-tat trade battles, was <a href="https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/fact2_e.htm">purposely designed to eliminate trade wars</a>, since they typically make us all worse off. And the trade liberalization that followed worked, <a href="https://www.aei.org/carpe-diem/how-significant-are-economic-gains-from-international-trade-since-wwii-2t-in-increased-us-gdp-18k-per-household/">delivering enormous wealth</a> to the U.S. and the world economy in the years since.</p>

<p>I believe it would be a shame if we returned to those days, and the unfortunate economic consequences that came with them.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290569/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Why the US-Canada trade war could change how American farmers grow their crops for years</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756494/original/file-20260827-50-g4gjo3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5602%2C3734&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Most healthy soybean fields like this one in Minnesota rely on fertilizer.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/agriculture-field-of-healthy-mid-growth-soybeans-in-late-news-photo/2163448535">Richard Hamilton Smith/Design Pics Editorial/Universal Images Group via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada is getting personal for American farmers.</p>

<p>After trade talks between the two longtime allies fell apart in mid-August 2026, Trump imposed <a href="https://apnews.com/article/canada-us-trade-tariffs-trump-857ef76b20a766e370d70176135b678e">50% tariffs on a wide range of Canadian imports</a> worth roughly US$20 billion (CAD$27 billion). Canada responded on Aug. 25, 2026, by announcing its own plan to put retaliatory <a href="https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/news/2026/08/list-of-products-from-the-united-states-subject-to-counter-tariffs-effective-september-8-2026.html">tariffs of 15% to 50%</a> on the same value of U.S. goods, effective Sept. 8.</p>

<p>Canada’s list includes dairy products and agricultural equipment, and there is an unspoken threat that it could expand to a crucial component in fertilizer that U.S. farmers rely on.</p>

<p>I have <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=5ioJPGUAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">studied agriculture and water quality</a> for more than a decade, including whether <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7158438">trade rules</a> change how farmers manage their land. </p>

<p>In my assessment, the enduring effect of this trade war on U.S. agriculture, if it continues to escalate, won’t be a single bad season. Across thousands of farms, farmers may have to reduce their fertilizer use as prices – already <a href="https://www.potatogrower.com/2026/08/why-higher-fertilizer-prices-are">high from supply disruptions</a> because of the war in Iran – rise. It may have little visible consequence at first, but the lasting impact could emerge later in smaller future harvests if this trade war continues.</p>

<h2>Are Canada’s tariffs aimed at farmers?</h2>

<p>Canada’s tariffs aren’t directly aimed at farmers, but farms will feel the cost if they go into effect.</p>

<p>A <a href="https://theconversation.com/tariffs-101:-what-they-are-who-pays-them-and-why-they-matter-now-271576">tariff is a tax</a> on imported goods paid by the importer, effectively raising the cost of those goods. When China responded to U.S. tariffs during the first Trump administration in 2018, its retaliatory tariffs hit U.S. soybeans and automobiles, directly affecting the American agricultural sector. Research shows <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/agec.70046">U.S. agricultural exports to China fell</a> by $7 billion to $10 billion a year, as Chinese buyers shifted to Brazilian suppliers.</p>

<p>Canada’s tariff list for Sept. 8 appears to match U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar. I believe agriculture is caught in the broader fallout, not directly targeted.</p>

<p>However, the effect will still reach farms.</p>

<p>Canada is one of the largest markets for American food, <a href="https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/chart-gallery/58374">importing about $28 billion</a> in U.S. agricultural products in 2025. Both <a href="https://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/international-markets-us-trade/countries-regions/usmca-canada-mexico/canada-trade-fdi">U.S. and Canada are also deeply integrated</a> in agricultural trade and farm equipment markets. Farm equipment is assembled from parts that cross the border. Live cattle and processed foods also move both ways. </p>

<p>Tariffs can raise costs along that chain. Canadian officials, recognizing that, included several billion dollars in <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/canada-retaliatory-tariffs-set-to-impact-20-billion-of-american-goods/">aid for their farmers</a> in announcing the tariff plan.</p>

<p>An <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5662091">analysis of the tariffs Trump ordered</a> in 2025 on countries around the world shows how fast agricultural trade flows reorganize under this sort of pressure. When North American trade barriers go up, U.S. imports of fruits and vegetables from Canada and Mexico typically drop, with buyers turning to Australia and Argentina instead. The result is often higher consumer prices for key agriculture products in the United States.</p>

<h2>The fertilizer risk</h2>

<p>Canada is also a major source of <a href="https://www.blm.gov/programs/energy-and-minerals/mining-and-minerals/nonenergy-leasable-materials/potash">potash</a>, a fertilizer ingredient that U.S. farmers depend on.</p>

<p>If pushed too far, Canada could levy <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/world/canada/canada-tariffs-trump-carney-retaliatory.html">export tariffs on potash</a> and, potentially, even on oil, natural gas and electricity, raising the price for U.S. buyers. The widespread impact that such a move would have on U.S. consumer prices may give Canada leverage going forward.</p>

<p>Crops require three main nutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Potassium comes <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/centers/national-minerals-information-center/potash-statistics-and-information">almost entirely from potash</a>. American mines <a href="https://www.statista.com/statistics/1376220/worldwide-largest-potash-producing-nations/?srsltid=AfmBOoqDcAtc6saCK5kaRcWM04jLZltEXf2st2ACMDRcPPBuJtoUfvl-">produce less than 1%</a> of the global potash supply, and the <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/news/technical-announcement/plenty-potash-some-regions-lack-low-cost-sources-crop-production">U.S. imports more than 80%</a> of its potassium from the Elk Point Basin in Saskatchewan, Canada. These are geology-based U.S. constraints in agriculture.</p>

<p>Notably, potash was not included in the U.S. tariff list. Taxing such a key agricultural input would have raised costs for American growers. </p>

<h2>How trade policy changes growing decisions</h2>

<p>American farmers are already squeezed on fertilizer costs. </p>

<p>When the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran shut down shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, it cut off a large source of nitrogen fertilizer, raising fertilizer and fuel prices. A Farm Bureau survey in April 2026 found <a href="https://www.fb.org/intel/markets/farm-bureau-survey-reveals-real-impact-of-fertilizer-availability-and-price">70% of farmers said they couldn’t afford</a> all the fertilizer they needed during spring planting. </p>

<p>Nitrogen washes out of soil and must be reapplied every year. Potassium and phosphorus, on the other hand, build up as a reserve. This means that a farmer facing high prices can skip an application and briefly live off that reserve. This is consistent with <a href="https://extension.missouri.edu/news/managing-potassium-and-phosphorus-when-prices-are-high-0">advice from agricultural extension researchers</a> who compare this coping strategy to a fuel gauge: You can make a trip or two without refilling, but not the third.</p>



<p>Potash was the one major nutrient that the Iran shock didn’t directly affect. However, if Canada raises the price of potash, that <a href="https://farmdocdaily.illinois.edu/2026/03/strait-of-hormuz-closure-and-fertilizer-supply-risks-for-us-agriculture.html">could have similar effects</a>.</p>

<p>When fertilizer prices spike, farmers tend to cut phosphorus and potassium first and nitrogen last. But restoring potassium in <a href="https://extension.illinois.edu/crops/soil-potassium">soil takes time</a>, with several pounds of fertilizer for every pound of soil-test potassium recovered, spread over years. So, even a one-year restriction on potash access can have an impact.</p>

<h2>Uncertainty has an effect on farmers’ choices</h2>

<p>Economic research shows that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/aepp.13083">trade policy uncertainty affects agricultural decisions</a> even before tariffs take effect. A farmer who cannot predict next year’s costs may delay the purchase and hope that prices will ease. </p>

<p>Fertilizer is often bought months ahead of planting, so hesitating in the fall can mean less goes on the ground in the spring. Uncertainty alone can reduce what gets applied before any tariff exists.</p>

<p>If U.S. farmers end up facing higher prices or short supplies for potassium fertilizer, the effects over time, including the chance of smaller yields, would arrive at the grocery store in the form of higher food prices long after the tariffs are likely to be lifted.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290504/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Why Democrats are amplifying corruption talk: A historical strategy for parties out of power</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755777/original/file-20260824-50-gq7pry.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6961%2C4640&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The public is always a little bit concerned about corruption, but not about particular actions by politicians.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/miniature-symbolic-residence-of-the-us-president-royalty-free-image/2166774286?phrase=political%20corruption&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Max Zolotukhin, iStock/Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>If you have seen campaign ads for the midterm elections, you have likely noticed that a major theme this year is corruption. </p>

<p>New Hampshire congressman and Senate candidate Chris Pappas has <a href="https://chrispappas.org/2026/07/fact-check-congressman-pappas-has-a-proven-record-of-taking-on-corruption-in-washington-and-fighting-for-ethics-reforms/">framed his campaign</a> around his anti-corruption efforts in Congress, claiming that his anti-corruption record includes the fact that he “doesn’t take a dime of corporate PAC money,” opposes congressional stock trading, and wants to ban companies from using AI to set prices based on Americans’ personal data. </p>

<p>A <a href="https://senateleadershipfund.org/press-releases/icymi-chris-pappas-ethics-questions-keep-mounting/">super PAC allied with Pappas’ prospective Republican opponent</a>, John Sununu, has run ads calling Pappas corrupt, alleging that Pappas “serves on a House committee that oversees Uber, where his husband, a former lobbyist, serves in an executive policy role.”  </p>

<p>This is one of many races where corruption has a prime role. On her <a href="https://dcinboxinsights.substack.com/">DCinbox Substack</a>, which tracks “how members of Congress communicate with constituents,” Lindsey Cormack shows that Democrats this year are talking about corruption six times as much as they did in 2022 and four times as much as Republicans have this year in their emails to constituents. This suggests that the corruption talk is a part of Democratic Party strategy.  </p>

<p>Why? </p>

<p>One possibility might be that <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/20/opinion/trump-doj-slush-fund-criminals-corruption.html">there is a lot of corruption happening</a>. Yet a puzzling feature of these advertisements is that few of them mention President Donald Trump, despite <a href="https://www.citizensforethics.org/reports-investigations/crew-reports/tracking-trumps-visits-to-his-properties-and-other-conflicts-of-interest/">plentiful allegations</a> of corrupt acts by Trump and members of his administration. </p>

<p>Another might be that the public is particularly concerned about corruption. Research shows, however, that the public is <a href="https://data4democracy.substack.com/p/the-democrats-path-forward-become">always a little bit concerned about corruption</a>, and that these worries often do not correspond with particular actions by politicians.</p>

<p>So what is going on, then? </p>

<p>The talk, it turns out, is not really about specific, identifiable corruption. It’s about delegitimizing your opponent.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/RLZYIJkFXjo?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Democratic congressional candidate Cait Conley says, ‘What we’re seeing from politicians today is not courage, it’s corruption.’</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Choice of those out of power</h2>

<p>My recent book, “<a href="https://tupress.temple.edu/books/american-corruption-talk">American Corruption Talk</a>,” co-authored with Molly Brigid McGrath, analyzes the prevalence of what we call “corruption talk” by presidents and presidential candidates since the nation’s founding. We argue that corruption talk is different from talk about real corruption – many Americans identify things as being corrupt even when they do not meet the textbook definition of corruption.  </p>

<p>In our book, we identify three types of corruption:</p>

<p>• Transactional corruption is inherent in particular acts – offering or accepting a bribe, for instance. </p>

<p>• Moral corruption is being a rotten person – someone who is corrupt is not trustworthy, even if we cannot identify anything specific that person has done wrong. </p>

<p>• Systemic corruption has to do with the government’s behavior itself. It is not a matter of bad people but bad institutions.</p>

<p>Corruption talk blurs the distinctions between these three distinct things. </p>

<p>In the book, we explore changes over time in how presidents, presidential candidates and party platforms discuss corruption. </p>

<p>We found that parties out of power talk much more about corruption than those who are in power. Corruption talk is popular among politicians who want to avoid taking strong ideological positions or tying themselves closely to their party leaders. They can use it as <a href="https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=1987831001919550">evidence of bipartisanship</a>, as a way to say they are <a href="https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=2273419230072483">not career politicians</a>, or to emphasize their <a href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DbFPxiVk04w/">competence and integrity</a>.</p>



<p>Corruption is what political scientists call a <a href="https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803115048341">valence issue</a> – almost everyone thinks corruption is bad, but not everyone agrees about how much of it there is. </p>

<p>Corruption talk, it turns out, is useful for bringing together parties or candidates who want to avoid talking about divisive issues. It is also a way to delegitimize the opposition. If one’s opponents are corrupt, it doesn’t matter what they say. They’re the kind of people who would do corrupt things, even if they haven’t done them yet.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755794/original/file-20260824-50-jz67sb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large fat man in a three piece suit with a bag of money for a head." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755794/original/file-20260824-50-jz67sb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755794/original/file-20260824-50-jz67sb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=636&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755794/original/file-20260824-50-jz67sb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=636&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755794/original/file-20260824-50-jz67sb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=636&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755794/original/file-20260824-50-jz67sb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755794/original/file-20260824-50-jz67sb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/755794/original/file-20260824-50-jz67sb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Deriding political corruption is an old American custom, as this 1874 Thomas Nast cartoon lampoons the corrupt New York administration led by ‘Boss’ Tweed and the Tammany Society.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/harpers-weekly-political-cartoon-lampoons-the-corrupt-new-news-photo/615221882?adppopup=true">Corbis via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Democrats avoid division</h2>

<p>The Democrats’ corruption talk of 2026 checks all of these boxes. </p>

<p>Democrats have internal divisions, from <a href="https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2026/08/20/whose-party-democratic-socialists-of-america/">political ideology</a> to <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/07/31/nx-s1-5896216/democrats-israel-congress-2026-midterm-elections">policy on Israel</a>, which they may wish to avoid talking about. </p>

<p>Talking about things Trump has done requires too much explanation – it’s hard to describe the Constitution’s <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R45992">foreign emoluments clause</a> in a 30-second ad. That clause bars the president from accepting “‘any present, Emolument, Office, or Title, of any kind whatever’ <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R45992">from a foreign government unless Congress consents</a>,” and <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/emoluments-clauses-explained">Trump has been accused of violating it</a>. </p>

<p>But talking about corruption in a moral or systemic sense – observing that the country is in decline, or that elites are out of touch – can be effective.</p>

<p>“To every Utahn tired of chaos and corruption, there’s a place for you on this campaign,” Ben McAdams, a former Democratic congressman from Utah and current candidate for the House, <a href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DbFPxiVk04w/">declared in a July 2026 Instagram post</a>.</p>

<p>So talking about corruption is a way to talk about Trump and the Trump administration without mentioning them directly. Voters unhappy with Trump will assume corruption talk is an indictment of Trump, while Trump supporters may assume the corruption is elsewhere – after all, Trump won the 2016 election, in part, by <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/nov/09/how-did-donald-trump-win-analysis">promising to take on the corrupt establishment</a>. </p>

<p>These distinctions – real corruption vs. corruption talk – go back at least to the country’s founding, if not beyond. Historically, corruption talk has stood in for other things. </p>

<p>For instance, <a href="https://www.loc.gov/classroom-materials/united-states-history-primary-source-timeline/progressive-era-to-new-era-1900-1929/overview/">the Progressive Era of the late 19th and early 20th centuries</a>, a time when activists in both parties worked together to pursue reforms in government, economic policy and social policy, was the era in which we find that corruption talk was most prevalent in American politicians’ rhetoric. It was also a moment when America was almost as <a href="https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262134644/polarized-america/">polarized and economically unequal as it is today</a>, and many Americans saw this inequality as a symptom of corruption.</p>

<p>None of this is to deny that the U.S. currently has a president who has engaged in <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/24/magazine/corruption-voters-trump-midterms.html">more overt acts of corruption</a> than any other. Trump’s actions – from his family’s documented <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/spotlight/trump-worlds-self-enrichment">cryptocurrency profiteering</a> to his appointment of a Cabinet <a href="https://campaignlegal.org/trump-administration-conflicts-of-interest">full of conflicts of interest</a> (such as stock ownership in companies regulated by their agencies, or a history of lobbying the very agencies they now run), to his <a href="https://www.pbs.org/video/what-is-known-about-trump-s-relationship-with-epstein-1752959275/">alleged ties</a> to the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein – no doubt have catalyzed this discussion. </p>

<p>Yet it is perhaps fitting that the nation’s 250th anniversary has been characterized by a return to a classic American preoccupation: the traditional American pastime of corruption talk.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289463/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: In taking Syria off state sponsor of terrorism list, US is putting its faith in al-Qaida alumni – that presents risks and opportunities

<title>In taking Syria off state sponsor of terrorism list, US is putting its faith in al-Qaida alumni – that presents risks and opportunities</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756345/original/file-20260826-60-rnh149.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=58%2C109%2C4957%2C3304&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">U.S. President Donald Trump meets Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Turkey on July 8, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-donald-trump-meets-syrian-president-ahmed-al-news-photo/2284641740?adppopup=true">Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Syria’s <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/us-removes-syrias-designation-state-sponsor-terrorism-2026-08-24/">delisting as a state sponsor of terrorism</a> was a long time coming.</p>

<p>The country had, after all, been on the U.S. State Department <a href="https://www.state.gov/state-sponsors-of-terrorism">list of proscribed nations</a> since it was created in 1979 – the only nation originally listed still on it. </p>

<p>That was until Aug. 24, 2026, when U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio <a href="https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/08/rescission-of-syrias-designation-as-a-state-sponsor-of-terrorism/">formally rescinded</a> Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism.</p>

<p>The shift removes barriers to American investment in Syria. But for the U.S. administration, it is also a bet on an unlikely figure.</p>

<p>Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa <a href="https://www.durham.ac.uk/research/current/thought-leadership/2025/11/how-former-jihadist-ahmed-al-sharaa-ended-up-being-welcomed-to-the-white-house/">was a designated terrorist</a> until November 2025 – it was my office within the State Department that <a href="https://2009-2017.state.gov/r/pa/prs/ps/2013/05/209499.htm">designated him in May 2013</a> under the name <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/01/2025-21680/revocation-of-the-designation-of-muhammad-al-jawlani-as-a-specially-designated-global-terrorist">Muhammad al-Jawlani</a>. </p>

<p>In delisting Syria, the U.S. administration is wagering that the former Islamist militant has changed and can work with the U.S. in areas of foreign policy, economics and even possibly defense.</p>

<h2>The rise and fall of a designation</h2>

<p>When the State Department created the state sponsor of terrorism list in <a href="https://scholarworks.lib.csusb.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1140&amp;context=history-in-the-making">December 1979</a> under the Export Administration Act, Syria joined fellow Middle Eastern countries Libya, Iraq and South Yemen on it.</p>

<p>By then, longtime Syrian leader <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/remembering-hafez-al-assad">Hafez al-Assad</a> had turned Damascus into a <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/deadly-connections/syria-and-palestinian-radical-groups/C600779615B293679041B4BA3A942830">headquarters for the Palestinian groups</a> that opposed any negotiated settlement with Israel. The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine General Command, the Abu Nidal Organization and Palestinian Islamic Jihad all operated from Syrian soil, and Hamas kept its external leadership in Damascus until 2012. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">

              <span class="caption">Syrian President Hafez al-Assad chats with Moammar Gadhafi of Libya in 1977.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/syrian-president-hafez-al-assad-and-muammar-al-qaddafi-of-news-photo/607379978?adppopup=true">Alain Nogues/Sygma/Sygma via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Syria was also the land bridge for Iranian weapons bound for Hezbollah in Lebanon. When I ran the State Department’s Office of Counterterrorism Finance and Designations from 2008 to 2018, Syria appeared in every annual Country Reports on Terrorism, and the entry rarely changed.</p>

<p>The Syrian <a href="https://sams-usa.net/syria-hub/syria-civil-war/">civil war that began during that period</a> eventually saw the demise of the Assad regime – Hafez’s son Bashar had continued his father’s hard-line legacy after coming to power in 2000. But it also saw the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/23/world/middleeast/syria-president-ahmed-al-shara.html">rise of al-Sharaa</a> as head of the Nusra Front, al-Qaida’s Syrian branch. Islamic State group founder <a href="http://csweb.brookings.edu/content/research/essays/2015/thebeliever.html">Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi</a> tasked al-Sharaa with building a beachhead in Syria for the terrorism network.</p>

<p>But when al-Baghdadi announced in <a href="https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/how-hayat-tahrir-al-sham-landed-us-terrorist-lists-and-why-it-should-stay-there-now">April 2013</a> that the Nusra Front would be folded into the Islamic State group, al-Sharaa refused and pledged allegiance to al-Qaida’s Ayman al-Zawahiri instead. He then broke with al-Qaida in 2016.</p>

<p>Ten years on, al-Sharaa was received at the <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-meets-syrias-president-historic-white-house-visit/story?id=127380173">White House</a> as a head of state, and the State Department <a href="https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2025/11/united-states-leads-effort-to-delist-syrian-leaders">removed him</a> from the terrorist list. </p>

<h2>A new course rife with risk</h2>

<p>The U.S. bet extends beyond one man. Syria’s security services were built from Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham, the successor group to the Nusra Front that al-Sharaa led to power in Syria. Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham was delisted by Rubio on the same day as Syria’s rescission.</p>

<p>Likewise, <a href="https://sana.sy/en/syria/2338458/">Syrian Interior Minister Anas Khattab</a>, who was a founding member of the Nusra Front, was delisted as a global terrorist on the same day as al-Sharaa. </p>

<p>The International Crisis Group <a href="https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/middle-east-north-africa/syria/struggle-pacify-syrias-foreign-legions">estimates that some</a> 5,000 foreign fighters remain under arms inside state forces. And the Soufan Center <a href="https://thesoufancenter.org/intelbrief-2026-january-8/">warned in January</a> that hard-liners within those services could break ranks and join the Islamic State group or other jihadist organizations. The Combating Terrorism Center at West Point <a href="https://ctc.westpoint.edu/from-insurgency-to-statecraft-al-sharaa-and-syrias-foreign-fighters-test/">reports</a> that veteran foreign jihadists now openly call al-Sharaa a sellout. </p>

<p>In short, al-Qaida’s alumni are not adjacent to the Syrian state – they are inside it. The Trump administration is betting that working with that grouping is worth the risk. Yet critics fear the consequences for the U.S. of allying with a Syria with such a high prevalence of former militants.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A man holds a cardboard banner with a man's face and the words 'Terrorist' on it." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756347/original/file-20260826-50-nwuves.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756347/original/file-20260826-50-nwuves.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756347/original/file-20260826-50-nwuves.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756347/original/file-20260826-50-nwuves.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756347/original/file-20260826-50-nwuves.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756347/original/file-20260826-50-nwuves.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756347/original/file-20260826-50-nwuves.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Another important implication is that once a country is removed from the State Department list, getting it back on is bureaucratically cumbersome. </p>

<p>It requires the secretary of state finding that a government has repeatedly provided support for acts of international terrorism. “Repeatedly” is the operative word. In my experience a designation needs a documented pattern, an intelligence record that survives interagency review, and a decision at the top of the government. Even on the quickest timelines, <a href="https://2017-2021.state.gov/u-s-announces-designation-of-cuba-as-a-state-sponsor-of-terrorism/">like for Cuba in 2021</a>, it is a cumbersome process. And until that designation were to go back into effect, sanctions relief would keep flowing.</p>

<h2>The strategic case for delisting</h2>

<p>Supporters of delisting, however, have a reasonable geostrategic argument to make. The Assad family <a href="https://www.rusi.org/explore-our-research/publications/commentary/russias-enduring-grip-syria">tied Syria to Moscow for half a century</a> – bases at Tartus and Khmeimim gave the Kremlin its only military footprint on the Mediterranean. </p>

<p>A Syrian government that is friendly with the West and accepts American security assistance has less reason to lean on Russia. And every step Damascus takes toward Washington is a step away from Moscow. </p>

<p>Yet, the Trump administration cashed in Washington’s best chip with Syria’s removal from the state sponsor of terrorism list. Russia, for the time being, still has <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2025/11/10/middleeast/syrias-postwar-pivot-reaches-washington-intl">boots on the ground in Syria</a>, and al-Sharaa <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2025/10/15/world/syria-al-sharaa-putin-moscow-visit-intl">visited Vladimir Putin in October 2025</a>.</p>

<p>If the Trump administration had waited until the end of 2026 to remove Syria from the state sponsor of terrorism list, it could have ensured that <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/syria-russia-reach-deal-future-tartous-hmeimim-bases-after-18-months-talks-2026-08-09/">Russia vacated</a> the military bases in Syria first.</p>

<p>But the U.S. president is keen to rush Syria into becoming an ally to Washington, not least because it would further isolate Iran, denying Tehran the influence it had under the Assad regime.</p>

<h2>The remaining calculi</h2>

<p>The Trump adminsistration’s policy shift could also have major domestic repercussions. Trump has been photographed with al-Sharaa in Riyadh and in the Oval Office. Those images are an asset while Syria adheres to Washington’s wishes. But they are a liability the moment it does not. </p>

<p>And the record already holds warnings. Government-aligned forces <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/03/10/syria-end-coastal-killing-spree-protect-civilians">killed Alawite civilians on the Syrian coast</a> in March 2025 and <a href="https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2026/03/un-syria-commission-releases-report-july-massacres-and-other-grave">Druze civilians in Suwayda in July 2025</a>. These were abuses of state power under al-Sharaa’s authority.</p>

<p>For Syria, the calculus is mostly positive. The State Department’s prior designation carried a ban on defense exports, controls on dual-use goods, limits on foreign assistance, and financial restrictions that made international banks treat Syria as untouchable. </p>

<p>Comprehensive sanctions ended in June 2025; the designation was the last major legal barrier to American investment.</p>

<p>The delisting also opens the door to a counterterrorism partnership. Syria <a href="https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/08/rescission-of-syrias-designation-as-a-state-sponsor-of-terrorism/">joined the coalition against the Islamic State group</a> in November 2025 and has run operations against the terrorist group, al-Qaida and Hezbollah networks.</p>

<p>Al-Sharaa’s past with the Islamic State group is the reason he wants it destroyed; the group spent years trying to <a href="https://english.alarabiya.net/News/middle-east/2025/11/10/syria-foiled-isis-plots-on-president-alsharaa-s-life-sources-say">kill him after the 2013 split</a>. His hatred of the Islamic State group appears genuine, and American cooperation with Damascus against the terrorist network will benefit the Syrians who suffered most under its rule. </p>

<p>One further consequence deserves consideration. Syria is the first state to leave the list after a once-designated terrorist replaced a designated regime. Other individuals classified as terrorists by the U.S. might well notice that the road from the list to the Oval Office can be short – and rewarding.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290468/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Why “Lake America” isn’t funny
excerpt: Donald Trump displays a map labeling Lake Ontario as "Lake America" in the Oval Office of the White House on August 27, 2026. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This
body: Donald Trump displays a map labeling Lake Ontario as "Lake America" in the Oval Office of the White House on August 27, 2026. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump says he’s renaming Lake Ontario

Let’s talk about it.  Can he really do that? Probably, though it doesn’t mean anyone will listen.  Strictly speaking, Trump’s executive order, signed Thursday in the Oval Office, directs the Interior Department to update the lake’s name to “Lake America” in the US’s Geographic Names Information System
It remains to be seen whether products like Apple and Google maps will follow suit, but New York Gov

Kathy Hochul, whose state contains the US portion of the lake, says she won’t .  Why is he doing that? The immediate answer is that Trump launched a trade war with Canada over the weekend, and he’s mad that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney won’t give him what he wants; this is a petty way to lash out.  That doesn’t explain the trade war itself, though
Unfortunately, when my colleague, noted Canadian resident Zack Beauchamp, went looking earlier this week, he couldn’t find an explanation either

As he writes , there’s absolutely no constituency for this fight — other than Trump’s own imperial desires as he keeps joking-but-maybe-not-joking about making Canada the 51st state.  Isn’t this just a stupid stunt? It’s a stupid stunt — but not just that
As my colleague Caitlin Dewey wrote earlier this week and Zack can attest, Canadians are royally pissed at the US

The trade war might feel like one more Trump fit of pique to Americans, but for Canadians, it’s a serious threat.  Thursday’s executive order further ratchets up those tensions, and it specifically plays into the (very credible) school of thought that Trump isn’t really in this to redress US-Canada trade imbalances; as with many things Trump, it’s about dominance and the desire to claim a “win” at any cost
Lastly, it’s worth dwelling for a second on the stunt itself
One, Lake Ontario isn’t Canada’s name for it; it predates either country
And two, ad hoc renaming of bodies of water — this isn’t even the first time this Trump term — puts Trump in some fairly uncomfortable company
And with that, it’s time to log off… My colleague Sara Herschander just debuted her new newsletter, Nice Things, which feels like a great fit for this section
It’s all about dreaming big to build a better America, one with widespread high-speed rail, affordable housing, and infrastructure that works
You can subscribe here and read a story from the first edition here
Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you back here tomorrow!

title: The weird coalition taking on Flock

body: A Flock camera photographed in Costa Mesa, California, on August 17, 2026. | Paul Bersebach/Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
I passed five Flock cameras on my drive to work today, entirely without realizing it

The AI-powered license plate readers have metastasized on light poles and roadside posts across the country over the past few years, building a vast national database of vehicle movements that law enforcement agencies can access with few restrictions.  What are they doing with all that data? Who has access, and for how long? We don’t have clear answers to these questions — and lawmakers on both the right and the left increasingly want them
Yesterday, Senate Republicans opened an inquiry into Flock’s data “collection, retention, and dissemination” practices — a first step that could eventually lead to federal regulation
State officials have also called for restrictions: The technology is “out of control,” Florida Gov
Ron DeSantis said during a Wednesday press conference.  It is one of maybe three times, I would hazard, that DeSantis and Vermont Sen

Earlier this month, the independent senator also warned that Flock knows when you’re going to the doctor or dropping your kid off at school, among other things.  For many Americans, his warning was no exaggeration: There are now 120,000 Flock cameras on US roads
You can use the crowdsourced map DeFlock to check your area
Go a little deeper View Link As the existence of a crowdsourced anti-Flock map might attest…people really do not like these cameras
In Tennessee this month, one conservative county commissioner went so far as to call for the hanging of Flock’s CEO
Even data centers rarely attract that level of vitriol
But as with data centers, both sides can find something to hate here , the longtime tech reporter Jason Koebler recently told Vox
On the right, critics typically attack the cameras as government overreach: “‘This is invasive government

Don’t surveil me,’” Koebler paraphrased.  On the left, critics frequently link the cameras to corporate surveillance, racist policing, the erosion of abortion rights, and immigration enforcement: “This protest is about more than license plate readers,” one progressive activist recently put it . “It’s about…mass surveillance as a tool for fascism and political persecution.” The issue has surfaced in midterm races in states including Florida , Ohio , and Michigan, where some candidates have sought to link their opponents — fairly or unfairly — to Flock
In Michigan, for instance, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed released a campaign video last week that suggested voters could “thank” his opponent for the proliferation of the cameras
That video includes footage from a hearing Rogers chaired in 2013, before Flock was even founded; Rogers has not publicly responded

Political responsibility for the cameras is complicated, of course: Flock typically inks its contracts with cities, counties, and local police departments, which state and national lawmakers don’t approve.  But they could certainly limit the use of automated plate readers in other ways, like requiring warrants for accessing data, limiting how long information is saved, and banning the cameras near schools, churches, abortion clinics, and other sensitive places.  One link for later ➨ Put your phone away
Clubs, bars, music venues, and other social spaces are increasingly hosting “phone-free” gatherings — an attempt to break free from the distraction and surveillance of our screens
These things are popping up everywhere, so chances are you can find one somewhere near you

But if not, it’s pretty easy to throw your own phone-free game night or book club, too.  Before you go… Did you know… that women experiencing cardiac arrest are 14 percent less likely than men to receive CPR? Bystanders are apparently less comfortable performing the procedure on people with breasts, which has prompted calls for better-endowed CPR training manikins
Today’s trivia: What city serves as the headquarters of the National Collegiate Athletic Association? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the stage name of the singer Paul David Hewson
That would be Bono, which is short for “Bono Vox” — a childhood nickname inspired by a Dublin hearing-aid shop.
